scenarios.title: The address on the envelope
scenarios.situation: A junior tech asks: 'When a packet travels, which OSI layer is responsible for the IP addresses that get it across networks?'
scenarios.prompt: Which layer — and why does the distinction matter for troubleshooting?
choices: Layer 3, the Network layer — IP addressing and routing live here; layer mix-ups send you to the wrong tools
Layer 2, the Data Link layer — IP addresses are MAC addresses
Layer 4, the Transport layer — ports are the same as IP addresses
Layer 7, the Application layer — DNS handles all addressing
scenarios.why: IP addresses belong to Layer 3 (Network): they provide logical, hierarchical addressing that routers use to forward between networks. Layer 2 MAC addresses only matter within a single broadcast domain. The distinction matters because a Layer 3 problem (wrong subnet, bad gateway) needs completely different tools than a Layer 2 problem (bad cable, duplex mismatch).
scenarios.hint: MAC addresses get a frame across one wire; what gets a packet across ten networks?

scenarios.title: The video call versus the file
scenarios.situation: You are choosing transport protocols: a live video call and a payroll file transfer, both crossing the WAN.
scenarios.prompt: Which protocol suits each, and why?
choices: UDP for the video call (speed over perfection), TCP for the file (every byte must arrive intact and in order)
TCP for both — reliability is always the priority
UDP for both — speed is always the priority
It does not matter; the application decides nothing
scenarios.why: TCP is connection-oriented with sequencing, acknowledgments, and retransmission — perfect for a file where one flipped byte corrupts payroll. UDP skips all that overhead for speed — perfect for live video, where a late packet is useless anyway and the codec conceals small losses. Choosing the transport is choosing which guarantee matters.
scenarios.hint: What is worse: a video frame that arrives late, or a paycheck byte that arrives wrong?

scenarios.title: The two-kilometer link
scenarios.situation: Two campus buildings 2 km apart need a 10 Gbps link. The conduit is already in place, but copper Ethernet maxes out at 100 meters.
scenarios.prompt: What medium do you specify?
choices: Single-mode fiber — designed for long distances, using laser light over kilometers
Cat6a copper — it can be stretched to 2 km with signal boosters
Multimode fiber — cheaper, and distance does not matter for fiber
Coaxial cable — it was good enough for the old network
scenarios.why: Single-mode fiber uses a narrow core and laser light to carry signals for kilometers — it is the standard answer for campus and metro links. Multimode is cheaper but limited to hundreds of meters (fine inside a building, wrong between them). Copper cannot span 2 km at 10 Gbps no matter the category.
scenarios.hint: Copper taps out at 100 meters. Which glass is built for kilometers, and what lights it?

scenarios.title: The patch panel puzzle
scenarios.situation: You need to connect a switch's SFP fiber port to the fiber patch panel. The panel ports are small, square-ish, with a latch — two of them side by side per link.
scenarios.prompt: Which connector type do you order?
choices: LC — the small-form-factor latch connector standard for SFP fiber links
RJ45 — the standard for all switch connections
BNC — the bayonet connector for fiber
DB-9 — the serial connector, adapted for fiber
scenarios.why: LC (Lucent Connector) is the small-form-factor fiber connector with a latch, designed for SFP/SFP+ transceivers — the duplex pair you describe is the classic LC duplex. RJ45 is copper, BNC is coax, and DB-9 is serial. Matching the connector to the transceiver is day-one physical-layer literacy.
scenarios.hint: SFP cages are tiny. Which fiber connector was made tiny to match?

scenarios.title: The switch that took everyone down
scenarios.situation: A small office runs a star topology: every PC connects to one central switch. That switch fails at 10 a.m. and the whole office is offline.
scenarios.prompt: What does this teach about topology, and what is the fix?
choices: The central switch is a single point of failure — add redundancy: a second switch, dual uplinks, or NIC teaming on critical hosts
Star topologies are obsolete — rewire as a bus
The PCs should have been wireless instead
Topology does not matter; switches never fail
scenarios.why: A star's strength (simple, cheap, easy to troubleshoot) is also its weakness: the center is a single point of failure. The design lesson is redundancy where downtime hurts — a second switch, aggregated uplinks, or at minimum a cold spare on the shelf. Mesh topologies eliminate the SPOF but cost far more; engineering is choosing where the risk is acceptable.
scenarios.hint: One box, everybody dark. What is the name for that kind of risk?

scenarios.title: Why the router counts in binary
scenarios.situation: A trainee is frustrated: 'Why do I need binary? The addresses are already in decimal.' The address on the whiteboard is 192.168.1.0/24.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct explanation?
choices: The /24 is a count of binary 1-bits in the mask — you cannot understand what the prefix length means without binary
Binary is only for programmers; network techs never use it
Decimal is enough because routers display decimal
Subnet masks are random numbers assigned by the ISP
scenarios.why: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit binary number wearing a decimal costume — 192.168.1.0 is 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000. The /24 means the first 24 of those bits are network, and the mask 255.255.255.0 is twenty-four 1-bits followed by eight 0-bits. Every subnetting decision — how many subnets, how many hosts — is binary arithmetic, so the decimal is just the display format.
scenarios.hint: The slash is counting something. What is it counting, one by one?

scenarios.title: The packet's journey down the stack
scenarios.situation: A trainee mixes up the order: 'Does the IP header go on before or after the Ethernet header?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct encapsulation order as data moves down the OSI stack?
choices: Data -> segment (TCP) -> packet (IP) -> frame (Ethernet) -> bits on the wire
Data -> frame -> packet -> segment -> bits
Data -> bits -> frame -> packet -> segment
Data -> packet -> segment -> frame -> bits
scenarios.why: Encapsulation works top-down: the Transport layer wraps data into a segment (adding ports), the Network layer wraps that into a packet (adding IP addresses), the Data Link layer wraps that into a frame (adding MAC addresses), and the Physical layer transmits bits. Each layer's header is read by its peer on the other end — that is why the order is fixed.
scenarios.hint: Think of nested envelopes, each stamped by a different post office. Which office stamps first?

scenarios.title: Which Layer Is Actually Broken?
scenarios.situation: Users report they can't reach the company intranet by name, but they CAN reach it by IP address. They can also browse the public internet normally, ping the intranet server's IP, and other subnets work fine.
scenarios.prompt: Using the OSI model to isolate the fault, which layer is implicated?
choices: Layer 1 — a cable must be damaged
Layer 3 — IP routing is failing
Layer 7 (application-layer name resolution) — DNS is failing while Layers 1-3 demonstrably work
Layer 2 — the switch MAC table is corrupt
scenarios.why: The OSI model is a fault-isolation tool: working IP connectivity (ping by IP, internet browsing) proves Layers 1-3 are functional end-to-end. Name resolution failing while IP works isolates the fault to the application-layer service that maps names to addresses — DNS. Layer 1/2/3 faults would break IP connectivity too, not selectively break names. On the exam, 'works by IP, fails by name' is the canonical DNS-at-Layer-7 signature.
scenarios.hint: IP works, names don't — what service translates between them, and at which layer does it live?
objectives: Isolate faults with the OSI model
evidence: Isolated a name-resolution failure to the application layer using OSI reasoning

scenarios.title: Four subnets from one /24
scenarios.situation: You have 192.168.10.0/24 and need four equal subnets for four departments, each needing at least 50 host addresses.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct subnetting plan?
choices: Borrow 3 bits: /27 subnets, 30 usable hosts each
Use /30 subnets — 2 usable hosts each is plenty
Keep the /24 whole and assign departments by VLAN only
scenarios.why: Four subnets need 2 borrowed bits (2^2 = 4). The mask becomes /26 (255.255.255.192), each subnet holds 64 addresses minus network and broadcast = 62 usable hosts — comfortably over 50. The subnets fall on 64-address boundaries: .0, .64, .128, .192. Borrowing 3 bits would give 8 subnets of only 30 hosts — failing the requirement.
scenarios.hint: How many bits must you borrow to get four subnets — and how many hosts survive in each?
evidence: Requirement

Network: 192.168.10.0/24
Subnets needed: 4
Hosts per subnet: >= 50

scenarios.title: The point-to-point link
scenarios.situation: Two routers connect over a serial point-to-point link. You must assign the smallest possible subnet — wasting addresses here is sloppy.
scenarios.prompt: Which prefix is correct for exactly two usable host addresses?
choices: /30 (255.255.255.252) — 4 addresses, 2 usable: one per router
/24 — plenty of room for growth
/31 — the modern answer everywhere
/29 — 6 usable hosts, safe margin
scenarios.why: A point-to-point link has exactly two endpoints, so /30 gives 4 total addresses minus network and broadcast = 2 usable — a perfect fit with zero waste. (Some platforms support /31 for point-to-point per RFC 3021, but /30 remains the classic exam-safe answer for 'two usable hosts'.) Oversizing to /24 burns 252 addresses for nothing.
scenarios.hint: Two routers, two addresses needed. What is 2^2 minus the two reserved?

scenarios.title: The VLAN that leaked
scenarios.situation: Voice phones and PCs share one flat network. Broadcast traffic is heavy, and anyone with Wireshark can sniff voice calls.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct design change?
choices: Create separate voice and data VLANs with an 802.1Q trunk to the router for inter-VLAN routing
Buy a faster switch — bandwidth fixes everything
Change all IPs to a different subnet but keep one broadcast domain
Disable broadcast traffic on the PCs
scenarios.why: VLANs split one physical switch into multiple logical broadcast domains: voice in one, data in another. 802.1Q tags trunked frames so the router can route between VLANs while broadcasts stay contained — which also keeps voice traffic away from curious sniffers. New IPs alone change nothing about who hears broadcasts.
scenarios.hint: Broadcasts go everywhere the wire goes. How do you build walls without new wires?

scenarios.title: The scope that ran dry
scenarios.situation: New devices get 169.254.x.x addresses while older ones work fine. The DHCP scope shows 0 free leases.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the fix?
choices: Scope exhaustion — shorten the lease time, reconcile stale leases, and expand the scope
The DHCP server is hacked — wipe it
New devices need static IPs from now on
The switch is blocking DHCP — replace it
scenarios.why: Older devices hold valid leases while new ones get APIPA: the scope is exhausted, usually by stale leases held long past their usefulness. Shortening lease duration lets dead leases expire, reconciling clears the ghosts, and expanding the scope prevents recurrence. The pattern — some work, newcomers fail — is the fingerprint of exhaustion.
scenarios.hint: The old-timers have addresses and the newcomers do not. What ran out?

scenarios.title: Local yes, internet no
scenarios.situation: A PC pings everything on its own subnet but cannot reach anything beyond it — no internet, no other subnets.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely misconfiguration?
choices: Missing or wrong default gateway — the PC has no route off its subnet
Wrong DNS server
Bad Ethernet cable
The PC's IP is APIPA
scenarios.why: Reaching the local subnet proves the NIC, cable, IP, and mask are fine; failing beyond it means the PC does not know where to send off-subnet traffic — the default gateway's job. DNS would break names but not IPs, and a bad cable would break everything. The gateway is the door out of the subnet, and this PC cannot find it.
scenarios.hint: It can talk to its neighbors but not the next town. Who gives directions out of town?

scenarios.title: The IPv6 loopback
scenarios.situation: You are documenting the IPv6 addressing plan and need the loopback address for testing, plus the link-local range for neighbor discovery.
scenarios.prompt: Which are correct?
choices: Loopback ::1; link-local fe80::/10
Loopback 127.0.0.1; link-local 169.254.0.0/16
Loopback ::ffff:127.0.0.1; link-local 192.168.0.0/16
Loopback 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 is deprecated; use 127.0.0.1
scenarios.why: IPv6 loopback is ::1 (all zeros except the last bit — the compressed form of 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1), and link-local addresses live in fe80::/10, auto-configured on every interface for neighbor discovery. The 127.0.0.1 and 169.254.0.0/16 answers are IPv4 concepts wearing the wrong costume.
scenarios.hint: 128 bits, eight hextets, and a lot of zeros to compress. What is the shortest possible address?

scenarios.title: The warehouse Wi-Fi
scenarios.situation: A warehouse needs Wi-Fi for scanners. The 2.4 GHz band is crowded with neighboring networks; the space is large and open with high shelves.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best wireless design?
choices: Use 5 GHz with multiple APs on non-overlapping channels, WPA3-Enterprise, and a site survey for placement
One powerful 2.4 GHz AP at maximum power in the corner
Open Wi-Fi with no password for easy scanner onboarding
Hide the SSID — security through obscurity
scenarios.why: Warehouses need capacity and coverage: 5 GHz offers more non-overlapping channels and less neighbor interference, multiple APs with a proper site survey cover the shelving dead zones, and WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X gives per-device credentials instead of one shared passphrase on a clipboard. One max-power AP creates a loud, unreliable cell; open Wi-Fi invites everyone.
scenarios.hint: Big space, metal shelves, crowded airwaves. What beats one loud AP?

scenarios.title: Wiring the New Warehouse
scenarios.situation: A warehouse needs 12 new drops: 8 for PoE security cameras along a 90-meter run, 2 for APs in a high-interference area near the loading dock, and 2 uplinks between IDF closets 400 meters apart through conduit shared with power lines.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct media plan?
choices: Cat5e for everything — cheapest option that 'works'
Cat6A for the PoE camera runs (heat/bundle and distance headroom) and APs, plus multimode fiber for the 400m IDF uplinks (distance + EMI immunity in the power conduit)
Coaxial cable throughout for maximum shielding
Wireless bridges for everything to avoid cable runs
scenarios.why: Media selection is constraint-matching: 90m PoE camera bundles need Cat6A's headroom for heat dissipation and alien crosstalk (Cat5e at length limit with PoE bundles risks failures); the 400m IDF link exceeds copper's 100m limit outright, requiring fiber; and conduit shared with power lines means EMI, which fiber is immune to. Coax is obsolete for new Ethernet; all-wireless can't reliably backhaul PoE cameras. Each choice follows from a physical constraint, not brand preference.
scenarios.hint: Three constraints: 100m copper limit, PoE heat in bundles, EMI near power — which media survives each?
evidence: Designed a mixed Cat6A/fiber plant matched to distance, PoE, and EMI constraints

scenarios.title: The blind NOC
scenarios.situation: The NOC cannot see device health — they learn about full disks and dead fans from users calling in. You need standardized remote monitoring of routers, switches, and servers.
scenarios.prompt: Which protocol and approach fit?
choices: SNMP — poll devices for metrics (CPU, interface counters, uptime) and receive traps on UDP 161/162
SMTP — email the devices and ask how they feel
FTP — download the health as a file every morning
Telnet — log into each device hourly and eyeball it
scenarios.why: SNMP is the standard for device monitoring: managers poll agents for OIDs covering CPU, memory, interface errors, and uptime, while agents fire traps to the manager on events. It is built for exactly this — fleet-wide, automated visibility — where manual logins and user complaints are not monitoring at all.
scenarios.hint: You need numbers from a hundred boxes without logging into any of them. What asks and listens?

scenarios.title: Slow — compared to what?
scenarios.situation: Users say 'the network is slow today.' Nobody can say what normal looks like — there are no recorded measurements of typical throughput, latency, or utilization.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and what do you do first?
choices: A performance baseline — measure normal first, then compare; without it, 'slow' is not a diagnosis
More bandwidth — slow always means buy bigger pipes
A new ISP — the current one is obviously at fault
Faster PCs for all users
scenarios.why: A baseline is the recorded normal: throughput, latency, jitter, utilization at known times. Without it you cannot distinguish a real degradation from a busy Monday, and every 'slow' report becomes a guessing game. Measure first, then the next complaint has something to be compared against.
scenarios.hint: Slow compared to what? If you cannot answer that, what can you not do?

scenarios.title: The outage with no map
scenarios.situation: A core switch fails and nobody knows which uplinks feed which closets — the only 'diagram' is in a former admin's head, and they left last year.
scenarios.prompt: What documentation would have prevented the scramble?
choices: Current physical and logical network diagrams plus labeled wiring and an asset inventory
A longer maintenance contract
More redundant hardware everywhere
A bigger whiteboard
scenarios.why: Physical diagrams show what connects to what and where; logical diagrams show addressing, VLANs, and routing; labeling and inventory tie them to reality. Together they turn an outage from archaeology into procedure. Redundancy helps availability, but documentation is what lets humans act correctly under pressure.
scenarios.hint: The map left with the person. What should never live only in a person?

scenarios.title: The single uplink
scenarios.situation: A branch office connects to headquarters over one router with one WAN link. When it flaps, the branch is an island.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct availability improvement?
choices: Add a redundant path — a second link and first-hop redundancy (HSRP/VRRP) so a failure fails over automatically
Buy a faster single link — speed is reliability
Schedule outages for nights so nobody notices
Give the branch a bigger switch
scenarios.why: High availability means no single point of failure in the path: a second WAN link plus first-hop redundancy (HSRP/VRRP) lets traffic fail over without human intervention. A faster single link is still a single link — speed does not survive a cut fiber. Design for failure, not just for load.
scenarios.hint: One wire, one island. What turns one wire into a path that survives?

scenarios.title: Logs everywhere, answers nowhere
scenarios.situation: Each switch and router keeps its own logs locally, which rotate away in days. After an incident, the evidence on the key device is already gone.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Centralized syslog — forward all device logs to a syslog server (UDP/TCP 514) with retention and search
Disable logging to save disk space
Log only errors, never informational messages
Copy logs by hand every Friday
scenarios.why: Centralized syslog gives every device's logs one home with retention, timestamps, and search — so post-incident forensics has evidence instead of rotated-away emptiness. Local-only logging with short rotation is the same as no logging the week after an incident. Severity filtering is fine, but centralization is the structural fix.
scenarios.hint: The evidence existed — for three days, on one box. Where should it have lived?

scenarios.title: The noon firmware upgrade
scenarios.situation: An admin wants to upgrade core switch firmware at noon 'because the window is quiet.' No rollback plan exists and users were not notified.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct process?
choices: Follow change management: risk assessment, maintenance window off-hours, tested rollback plan, stakeholder notification
Noon is fine if it is quick
Skip the rollback plan — firmware upgrades never fail
Just do not tell users; they will not notice
scenarios.why: Changes to production infrastructure go through change management: assess risk and impact, schedule a maintenance window when impact is lowest, have a tested back-out plan, and notify stakeholders. 'Quiet noon' is still production hours, and a failed upgrade without a rollback plan turns minutes of work into hours of outage.
scenarios.hint: If the firmware bricks the switch at 12:05, what is the plan at 12:06?

scenarios.title: The choppy calls
scenarios.situation: Voice calls break up every afternoon when backups run. Data throughput is fine — only real-time voice suffers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: Implement QoS — classify and prioritize voice traffic so backups cannot starve it
Buy more bandwidth — voice needs bigger pipes
Move backups to tape
Tell users to call in the morning instead
scenarios.why: This is a classic QoS case: bulk backup traffic saturates queues and voice — which needs low latency and jitter, not raw bandwidth — arrives late and choppy. QoS markings (DSCP) and priority queuing guarantee voice its slice regardless of the backup flood. More bandwidth helps until the next bulk job; prioritization fixes the actual contention.
scenarios.hint: The pipe is full of backups and the voice is drowning. Do you need a bigger pipe or a lifeguard?

scenarios.title: The Rogue DHCP Mystery
scenarios.situation: Half the office gets 192.168.99.x addresses and loses corporate access every morning around 9 AM. The corporate DHCP scope is 10.1.0.0/16. By 10 AM it resolves itself.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what is the definitive fix?
choices: DHCP scope exhaustion — expand the 10.1.0.0/16 scope immediately
A rogue DHCP server (someone's home router plugged in backwards) winning the race each morning — find it via DHCP snooping + Option 82, then implement DHCP snooping with trusted ports
DNS poisoning — flush DNS on all clients
The core switch is failing under morning load — replace it
scenarios.why: Wrong-subnet addresses at a consistent time = rogue DHCP server winning the race when clients boot. The 9 AM pattern matches arrivals powering on. The fix is DHCP snooping: trust only the uplink ports facing the legitimate server, drop DHCP offers on untrusted ports, and use Option 82 to trace the rogue's port. Scope exhaustion would give APIPA (169.254.x.x), not a foreign private subnet.
scenarios.hint: Clients get SOME address, just the wrong one. What device answers DHCP first wins — who is answering?
evidence: Client ipconfig
IPv4: 192.168.99.50, DHCP server: 192.168.99.1, lease obtained 08:57
Legitimate scope

scenarios.title: The Telnet rule
scenarios.situation: A firewall audit finds Telnet open to the internet on a router's outside interface. Credentials cross that session in cleartext.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct firewall action?
choices: Deny inbound TCP 23 from untrusted zones and require SSH (TCP 22) for remote administration
Leave Telnet open but change the password monthly
Block TCP 22 instead — SSH is the risky one
Open Telnet wider so admins can connect faster
scenarios.why: Telnet (TCP 23) sends everything — including usernames and passwords — in cleartext, so it has no place on an untrusted interface. The fix is a firewall rule denying inbound 23 from outside, with SSH (TCP 22, encrypted) as the administrative path. A stronger password on a cleartext protocol protects nothing from a sniffer.
scenarios.hint: The password is strong, but the wire is glass. What sees everything?

scenarios.title: Detect or prevent?
scenarios.situation: A security architect must choose between IDS and IPS for the data-center edge. The requirement: stop the attack in progress, not just log it.
scenarios.prompt: Which fits, and what is the trade-off?
choices: IPS — inline, it can drop malicious traffic; the trade-off is that a false positive can block legitimate traffic
IDS — it prevents attacks by detecting them loudly
Either — they are the same product with different names
Neither — firewalls already do this
scenarios.why: IDS is passive: it watches a copy of traffic and alerts. IPS sits inline and can actually drop or reset malicious sessions — which meets the 'stop it' requirement. The cost of inline prevention is risk: a false positive blocks real business traffic, so IPS tuning is an ongoing discipline, not a one-time install.
scenarios.hint: One watches and shouts; the other stands in the road. Which one can take the hit?

scenarios.title: The remote worker's tunnel
scenarios.situation: An employee working from home needs secure access to internal file shares. The traffic crosses the public internet.
scenarios.prompt: Which solution fits, and which VPN type is it?
choices: A client-to-site (remote-access) VPN — encrypted tunnel from the laptop to the corporate network
A site-to-site VPN between their home router and HQ
Port-forward SMB (TCP 445) directly through the firewall
Email the files back and forth instead
scenarios.why: Remote-access (client-to-site) VPNs exist for exactly this: one roaming user tunneling into the corporate network over encrypted IPsec or SSL/TLS. Site-to-site connects whole networks, not individuals. Exposing SMB to the internet is asking for ransomware, and email is not a file-access strategy.
scenarios.hint: One laptop, hostile internet, private shares. What wraps the laptop's traffic in armor?

scenarios.title: The evil twin
scenarios.situation: Users report a new open network named 'CorpWiFi-Free' with a stronger signal than the corporate SSID. Several laptops have auto-joined it.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what is the response?
choices: Rogue/evil-twin AP conducting on-path attacks — contain it, find it physically, and enforce WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation so clients reject impostors
It is just a helpful neighbor boosting our signal — thank them
Rename the corporate SSID to match it
Turn off all Wi-Fi to be safe
scenarios.why: An evil twin mimics the legitimate SSID to harvest credentials and intercept traffic — a classic on-path attack. Respond by locating the rogue device (wireless intrusion detection helps), removing it, and hardening clients: WPA3-Enterprise with proper server-certificate validation makes clients refuse the impostor instead of auto-joining it.
scenarios.hint: Same name, stronger signal, no password. What is it fishing for?

scenarios.title: The poisoned cache
scenarios.situation: Users' traffic to the gateway is intermittently redirected through an unknown MAC address. The gateway's IP now maps to two different MACs on different machines.
scenarios.prompt: What attack is this, and what mitigates it at the switch?
choices: ARP spoofing/poisoning — mitigate with Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) validating ARP against the DHCP snooping binding table
DNS spoofing — change the DNS servers
A routing loop — enable STP
Normal behavior — ARP always maps one IP to two MACs
scenarios.why: ARP has no authentication, so an attacker can poison caches and claim to be the gateway — the textbook on-path (man-in-the-middle) setup. Dynamic ARP Inspection on the switch checks every ARP packet against the trusted DHCP-snooping binding table and drops the lies. One IP mapping to two MACs is never normal.
scenarios.hint: ARP trusts everyone. What happens when someone lies — and who should check IDs at the door?

scenarios.title: The open closet
scenarios.situation: A wiring closet is accessible to anyone in the building. Unused switch ports are live, all ports are in the default VLAN, and the switch still uses factory credentials.
scenarios.prompt: What is the hardening checklist?
choices: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, assign ports to proper VLANs, enable port security — and lock the closet
It is an internal network, so no hardening is needed
Just change the credentials; the rest is overkill
Unplug the switch when not in use
scenarios.why: Physical access plus live unused ports is an open invitation: anyone can plug in and join the default VLAN. Hardening is layered — credentials, disabled ports, VLAN assignment, port security (limiting MACs per port) — and the cheapest control of all is a locked door. 'Internal' is not a security boundary once the closet is public.
scenarios.hint: The door is open and the ports are live. How many invitations is that?

scenarios.title: The flat network
scenarios.situation: A malware outbreak on one workstation spreads to every server in minutes — the entire company is one flat broadcast domain with no internal filtering.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural change contains the next outbreak?
choices: Network segmentation — VLANs and firewall zones separating workstations, servers, and sensitive systems so a compromise cannot roam freely
Faster antivirus on every machine
A bigger internet pipe
More frequent password changes
scenarios.why: Segmentation limits blast radius: when workstations, servers, and crown-jewel systems live in separate zones with firewall policy between them, malware that lands on a desktop cannot walk straight into the database. Endpoint tools help, but architecture is what turns one infected PC from a company-wide event into a contained incident.
scenarios.hint: One infected PC, whole company down. What walls were missing?

scenarios.title: The Rogue Switch in the Conference Room
scenarios.situation: Someone plugged a $20 unmanaged switch into a conference-room wall jack to connect extra laptops. Now the help desk sees intermittent outages: some users get IP addresses in a strange range, and the network team spots two devices claiming to be the default gateway.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what is the best preventive control?
choices: A broadcast storm; enable storm control
A rogue DHCP server on the cheap switch is handing out bad leases and a rogue gateway; enable DHCP snooping with trusted ports plus Dynamic ARP Inspection
The switch is too slow; replace it with a managed switch and leave the port open
Normal behavior; unmanaged switches are safe on enterprise networks
scenarios.why: The symptoms are textbook rogue DHCP: wrong IP ranges mean a second DHCP server is answering faster than the legitimate one, and a rogue gateway enables man-in-the-middle traffic interception. DHCP snooping builds a binding table of legitimate DHCP servers on trusted (uplink) ports and drops DHCP offers from untrusted access ports — killing the rogue server at the switch. Dynamic ARP Inspection uses that binding table to stop the gateway spoofing. Storm control addresses a different problem; replacing the switch without port controls just legitimizes the hole.
scenarios.hint: Wrong IPs plus a second 'gateway' — what device is answering requests it shouldn't, and what switch feature silences it?
evidence: Diagnosed rogue DHCP/gateway spoofing and prescribed DHCP snooping with DAI

scenarios.title: Where do you ping first?
scenarios.situation: A user has no network access. You sit down at their PC with the troubleshooting methodology in mind.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first-test order?
choices: Ping loopback (127.0.0.1), then the default gateway, then a remote host — inside out, isolating each segment
Ping a remote website first — if it works, everything is fine
Reinstall the NIC driver first — drivers are usually the problem
Replace the cable first — cables are usually the problem
scenarios.why: Inside-out testing isolates the fault's segment: loopback proves the local TCP/IP stack, the gateway proves the LAN path, a remote host proves routing and beyond. The first failure tells you exactly which segment to work in. Starting remote tells you only 'broken' — starting with parts replacement skips diagnosis entirely.
scenarios.hint: If the loopback fails, do you need to check the cable? Let the order answer.

scenarios.title: Where do the packets die?
scenarios.situation: A branch office cannot reach a cloud application. Ping to the app fails; ping to the local gateway works.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool pinpoints the failing hop?
choices: traceroute (tracert on Windows) — it lists each hop so you can see exactly where responses stop
ipconfig — it shows the failing hop
nslookup — it traces the route
netstat — it lists the hops
scenarios.why: Traceroute sends packets with increasing TTL values, forcing each router along the path to reveal itself — the last responding hop before the timeouts is where the path breaks. Ping only says 'unreachable'; traceroute says 'unreachable, and here is precisely where.' That turns a vague WAN ticket into a specific provider or device to engage.
scenarios.hint: Ping says no. Who says where?

scenarios.title: The name that will not resolve
scenarios.situation: Users can reach the new intranet server by IP but not by its hostname. You suspect DNS.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool queries DNS directly, and what do you check?
choices: nslookup (or dig) — query the hostname and confirm which server answers and what it returns
ping — it is the DNS testing tool
tracert — it resolves names hop by hop
arp -a — it shows DNS entries
scenarios.why: nslookup and dig speak DNS directly: they show which server answered and what record it returned, separating 'the record is wrong/missing' from 'the client is asking the wrong server.' Ping uses the resolver but does not interrogate it — when DNS is the suspect, question DNS itself.
scenarios.hint: The suspect is the phone book. Which tool reads the phone book directly?

scenarios.title: The link that died in the move
scenarios.situation: A workstation worked Friday, was moved to a new desk Monday, and now shows 'network cable unplugged'. The cable clicks into both ends.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic check?
choices: Verify link lights, try a known-good cable, confirm T568B on both ends with a cable tester, and try a different switch port
Reinstall Windows — moves corrupt the OS
Replace the workstation — moves kill PCs
Call the ISP — the internet is down
scenarios.why: A move changes exactly one thing: the physical path. Link lights give instant feedback, a known-good cable eliminates the most abused component, a tester verifies the pairs survived the move, and a different port rules out a dead jack. The methodology says test the changed thing first — everything else is untouched.
scenarios.hint: What is the only thing that changed between Friday and Monday?

scenarios.title: The slow, collision-filled link
scenarios.situation: A link negotiates at 100 Mbps but throughput is terrible; the switch shows rising collision and FCS error counters on that port.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely cause?
choices: Duplex mismatch — one side half-duplex, the other full-duplex
The cable is too short
Too much bandwidth is available
The switch needs a firmware upgrade
scenarios.why: In a duplex mismatch, the half-duplex side treats the full-duplex side's transmissions as collisions and backs off, while the full side never backs off — the result is exactly this: link up, throughput destroyed, collision and FCS counters climbing. The fix is matching duplex settings, normally by leaving both sides on auto-negotiation.
scenarios.hint: One side politely waits its turn; the other talks over it. What breaks?

scenarios.title: Works here, not there
scenarios.situation: An application works for users on the LAN but fails for users across the WAN. The server is up and the app listens on TCP 8443.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the check?
choices: A firewall in the path is blocking TCP 8443 — verify with a port test and check the listening socket with ss/netstat on the server
The application is broken for everyone
The WAN is down
Users need new PCs
scenarios.why: 'Works locally, fails remotely' is the signature of a path filter: something between the WAN users and the server is dropping TCP 8443. Confirm the server is actually listening (ss -tuln), then test the port from the remote side and walk the firewall rules in between. The app is proven working — the path is the suspect.
scenarios.hint: Same app, same server, different network — different result. What sits between them?

scenarios.title: The intermittent application
scenarios.situation: An application fails randomly — no pattern by time, user, or location. Logs show nothing conclusive.
scenarios.prompt: What is the deepest diagnostic step when all else is inconclusive?
choices: Capture packets with Wireshark at both ends and compare — the wire does not lie about retransmits, resets, or malformed traffic
Reboot everything weekly as preventive medicine
Blame the ISP without evidence
Rewrite the application
scenarios.why: When symptoms are intermittent and logs are silent, a packet capture is ground truth: you can see the actual TCP handshakes, retransmissions, resets, and timing that no log recorded. Capturing at both ends distinguishes 'never sent' from 'sent but lost.' It is the deepest tool because it observes reality instead of inferring it.
scenarios.hint: Everyone's logs say nothing. What sees everything that actually crossed the wire?

scenarios.title: Methodology: The Intermittent Drop
scenarios.situation: A branch office loses connectivity for 2-3 minutes, several times a day, then recovers on its own. The last tech 'fixed' it by rebooting the router, which changed nothing. You arrive with a structured methodology: identify, theorize, test, establish plan, implement, verify, document.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct next step after identifying the symptom pattern?
choices: Immediately replace the router — reboots suggest hardware failure
Theorize probable causes from the pattern (e.g., DHCP lease expiry, STP reconvergence, WAN flaps, scheduled interference) and test by correlating outage times with logs before changing anything
Reboot all network devices in sequence
Escalate to the ISP immediately
scenarios.why: The CompTIA troubleshooting methodology exists to prevent exactly what the last tech did — random action without theory. Intermittent, self-recovering drops point at time-correlated causes (DHCP lease timers, STP topology changes, cron-like interference), so the next step is forming probable-cause theories and testing them against logs/timestamps. Replacing hardware or rebooting everything without evidence wastes resources and can mask the real fault; ISP escalation comes after you've ruled out your own infrastructure with data.
scenarios.hint: The methodology step after 'identify the problem' is 'establish a theory' — what does the intermittent pattern suggest you check first?
objectives: Correlate intermittent faults with timed causes
evidence: Formed and log-tested theories for an intermittent outage instead of swapping hardware

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Comptia Network Plus as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Networking Concepts Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Networking Concepts is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Networking Concepts?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Networking Concepts issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Networking Concepts is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Networking Concepts supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Networking Concepts failure in Comptia Network Plus.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Networking Concepts
evidence: System Status
All Networking Concepts components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Packet Journey: LAN to WAN
scenarios.situation: A user opens a web page hosted in another country. The packet leaves the PC, crosses a campus LAN, passes the core, exits through the edge firewall and ISP router, and traverses the internet to the server.
scenarios.prompt: Walking the packet's journey, at which handoff does the source MAC address change while the source IP stays the same?
choices: At the user's PC when the packet is first created
At every router hop: each router strips the old Layer 2 frame and builds a new one with its own egress MAC, while the Layer 3 source IP is preserved end-to-end
At the firewall, which rewrites both MAC and IP
Never — MAC addresses are end-to-end like IP addresses
scenarios.why: This is the fundamental L2/L3 journey distinction: MAC addresses are hop-local (each router re-frames the packet for the next link with new source/destination MACs), while IP addresses are end-to-end (source IP stays the user's, destination IP stays the server's, across the whole journey — NAT aside). Visualizing the packet as a traveler that changes its 'local vehicle' (frame) at every router while keeping its 'passport' (IP) is the systems view that makes routing, ARP, and switching click together.
scenarios.hint: Frames are local to each link; packets are global — which header gets rewritten at each router?
objectives: Trace L2 vs L3 addressing across hops
evidence: Traced MAC rewrite vs IP preservation across router hops

scenarios.title: DNS Resolution Chain
scenarios.situation: A workstation needs to resolve www.example.com for the first time today. Its local DNS cache is empty, and the configured resolver has nothing cached either.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence of the resolution journey?
choices: Workstation asks the authoritative server directly, which answers immediately

Workstation → recursive resolver → root servers (where is .com?) → .com TLD servers (where is example.com?) → example.com authoritative server (what is www's IP?) → answer cached at each level on the way back
Workstation broadcasts on the LAN asking who knows www.example.com
The resolver guesses from its hosts file and returns that
scenarios.why: DNS resolution is a delegation chain walked top-down: the recursive resolver starts at the roots (which only know where TLD servers are), follows the referral to the .com servers (which only know example.com's nameservers), and finally asks the authoritative server that actually holds the www record. Each hop caches its answer, which is why the second lookup is instant — the systems view shows caching as the chain 'remembering' each handoff. Direct-to-authoritative skips how resolvers discover authority; LAN broadcast is LLMNR/NetBIOS, not DNS.
scenarios.hint: Nobody knows the full answer at first — who knows who to ask next, starting from the top?
objectives: Explain caching at each chain level
evidence: Sequenced root-to-authoritative DNS resolution with per-level caching

scenarios.title: DHCP Handshake: DORA in Motion
scenarios.situation: A laptop connects to the office Wi-Fi. It has no IP address. Within seconds it's online with address 10.20.30.45, gateway 10.20.30.1, and DNS servers — all assigned automatically.
scenarios.prompt: What is the four-step handshake that just happened, in order?
choices: Request → Offer → Discover → Acknowledge
Discover (broadcast: any DHCP server out there?) → Offer (server proposes an address) → Request (client claims it) → Acknowledge (server confirms lease with gateway/DNS options)
The AP assigns the address directly from its own pool
Authenticate → Associate → Encrypt → Address
scenarios.why: DORA is a negotiation journey: the client shouts into the dark (Discover broadcast — it has no address yet, so it must broadcast), servers answer with proposals (Offer), the client selects and formally claims one (Request — this step matters because it also handles declines/relays), and the server commits the lease plus options like gateway and DNS (Acknowledge). The AP is just a bridge — it doesn't assign addresses. Seeing it as discover-then-negotiate explains why DHCP fails across routers without a helper address (broadcasts don't cross routers).
scenarios.hint: The client starts with no address and must shout — what four messages turn that shout into a confirmed lease?
objectives: Explain why DHCP needs broadcast/helper addresses
evidence: Sequenced the DORA handshake and explained broadcast behavior

scenarios.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake Anatomy
scenarios.situation: A packet capture shows a client trying to open an HTTPS session: you see SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK — but immediately after, the client sends RST and the connection dies. The server admin insists 'the server is up and listening.'
scenarios.prompt: Reading the handshake as a system, what does the RST after a completed handshake tell you?
choices: The network dropped the handshake packets
The handshake completed (both sides agreed on sequence numbers), so the failure is above TCP — the application rejected the connection (e.g., wrong SNI/host, TLS failure, or app-level refusal)
TCP is unreliable and handshakes often fail randomly
The client's SYN was malformed
scenarios.why: The three-way handshake is TCP's agreement ceremony: SYN (here's my starting sequence number), SYN-ACK (acknowledged, here's mine), ACK (acknowledged) — after which both sides have synchronized state and the connection is ESTABLISHED. A RST after that point means TCP did its job and something higher up killed the session: the classic case is a TLS/SNI mismatch or an application with no listener on the requested host. The systems view separates 'the transport handshake worked' from 'the application refused' — different layers, different fixes.
scenarios.hint: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK all completed — so which layer's job is done, and which layer killed it?
objectives: Interpret the TCP handshake in captures
Separate transport success from application refusal
evidence: Diagnosed a post-handshake RST as application-layer refusal, not TCP failure

scenarios.title: VLAN Trunking Flow
scenarios.situation: Two switches connect via a single cable. Switch A has VLAN 10 (sales) and VLAN 20 (engineering) access ports; Switch B has the same VLANs. A sales PC on Switch A can't reach a sales server on Switch B, but engineering-to-engineering across the switches works fine.
scenarios.prompt: Following the frame's journey across the trunk, what is the most likely fault?
choices: The trunk cable is unplugged
VLAN 10 isn't allowed (or isn't tagged) on the trunk — the frame's 802.1Q tag for VLAN 10 is missing or pruned, so Switch B drops it, while VLAN 20's tags pass
The sales PC has the wrong IP address
Spanning tree blocked the trunk port
scenarios.why: A trunk carries multiple VLANs by tagging each frame with an 802.1Q VLAN ID as it crosses the inter-switch link — the tag is the frame's 'which broadcast domain do I belong to' label. If VLAN 10 is pruned from the allowed list or there's a native-VLAN mismatch affecting it, VLAN 10 frames die at the trunk while VLAN 20 flows normally — exactly the 'one VLAN works, one doesn't' symptom. A dead cable or blocked port would kill both VLANs; a wrong PC IP wouldn't be VLAN-selective across switches.
scenarios.hint: One VLAN crosses the link fine, the other doesn't — what per-VLAN mechanism on the trunk could differ?
evidence: Diagnosed selective VLAN failure as trunk allowed-list/tagging issue

scenarios.title: Routing Decision Chain
scenarios.situation: A router's table has: 10.0.0.0/8 via OSPF, 10.20.0.0/16 via a static route, 10.20.30.0/24 via EIGRP, and 0.0.0.0/0 toward the ISP. A packet arrives destined for 10.20.30.99.
scenarios.prompt: Walking the router's decision chain, which route wins and why?
choices: 0.0.0.0/0 — the default route is the ultimate fallback and always wins
10.0.0.0/8 via OSPF — OSPF has the best administrative distance
10.20.30.0/24 via EIGRP — longest prefix match wins regardless of protocol or AD
10.20.0.0/16 static — static routes beat dynamic protocols
scenarios.why: The routing decision chain has a strict order: first, longest prefix match (most specific network wins — /24 beats /16 beats /8 beats /0); only when two routes have the SAME prefix length does administrative distance break the tie. 10.20.30.0/24 is the most specific match for 10.20.30.99, so it wins before AD is ever consulted. This ordering is why route summarization and specific static overrides work — specificity outranks protocol preference every time.
scenarios.hint: The router checks prefix length before it ever compares protocols — which entry is most specific?
evidence: Selected the winning route via longest prefix match before administrative distance
