lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because N10-009 topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skimming lessons without attempting the knowledge check — verification is the learning, not a gate to dodge.
Doing scenarios before reading the domain lessons — scenarios assume the concepts; you will guess instead of reason.
Ignoring the Terminal labs — hands-on execution is what separates passing from failing on performance-based questions.
lessons.try_it: Open the Terminal tab now and type `whoami`. That is the smallest possible lab — you just proved the environment works.

lessons.title: N10-009 Exam Strategy
concepts: N10-009 tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in this bootcamp, cover the choices, and write what the question is really asking in one sentence before looking at options.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: subnetting drills daily (10 min) + 2 domains per week; mock at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.
lessons.try_it: Do one Feynman write right now: explain in 3 sentences what a bootcamp 'domain' is and why the order matters.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.
The Systems Anatomy explorer in Visuals lets you step through living systems click by click. Use it before each domain's scenarios.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'DNS resolves names to IPs.'
Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
example.walkthrough: One narrated journey demonstrates more competence than ten memorized definitions. Practice this voice in every scenario's 'why' explanation — read them aloud.

pitfalls: Defining terms instead of tracing flows when asked 'how does X work?'
Jumping to fixes before mapping the system — fixes applied to the wrong layer waste time and credibility.
Treating each domain as separate — the mock assessment deliberately chains them; practice connecting domains now.
lessons.try_it: Open the Systems Anatomy domain and step through one full system in the explorer before your first study session.

lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates N10-009 conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. Branch Office Network — a designed, subnetted, VLAN'd branch network with documentation
  2. Home Lab Network — VLANs, firewall rules, and VPN on real or virtual gear
  3. Network Monitor Dashboard — SNMP/flow collection with alerting on a lab network
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-paragraph project selection rationale now: which project, why it fits your goals, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.
lessons.try_it: Create your build log file now with today's date and your project title as the header.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire CompTIA Network+ Skills
concepts: The roles: Network Technician, NOC Analyst, Network Administrator, Field Engineer. Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

example.code:
Posting analysis template:
  Role: ___
  Repeated requirements (3+ postings): ___
  Nice-to-haves: ___
  My gaps: ___ → study priority
example.walkthrough: The job posting is the employer's requirements doc. Analyze it like one — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: Chasing titles instead of skill clusters — the same skills hide under five different titles.
Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

example.code:
Bullet formula: [Action verb] + [what] + [scale] + [outcome]
  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.

lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The CompTIA Network+ Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For CompTIA Network+, the essential categories:
  Simulation: Packet Tracer/GNS3
  Monitoring: Wireshark/PRTG
  Documentation: NetBox/draw.io
  Automation: Ansible

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: Subnetting at Exam Speed
concepts: Every subnet question answers four things: network address, broadcast address, first/last usable host, and host count. Train to produce all four from any CIDR in under 60 seconds.
The magic number method: for any octet, magic = 256 - mask octet. Multiples of the magic number are the subnet boundaries — the rest is arithmetic.
Classful boundaries are history; CIDR is the reality. /24 = 254 hosts, /25 = 126, /26 = 62, /27 = 30, /28 = 14, /29 = 6, /30 = 2. Memorize this table cold.
VLSM questions give a topology with different host counts per segment — always subnet the LARGEST requirement first, then fit smaller ones into the remaining space.
The 'borrowed bits' framing: a /26 borrows 2 bits from the host portion of a /24, creating 4 subnets of 62 hosts each. Think in borrowed bits, not memorized tables.

example.code:
192.168.10.0/26 → mask octet 192, magic = 256-192 = 64
  Subnets: .0, .64, .128, .192
  First subnet: network .0, broadcast .63, usable .1–.62 (62 hosts)
  Second: network .64, broadcast .127, usable .65–.126
example.walkthrough: Subnetting is a motor skill, not a memory task. Drill 10 subnets a day on paper until the magic-number method is automatic — the exam gives you no calculator for this.

pitfalls: Forgetting to subtract 2 for network and broadcast — 'how many hosts' always means usable hosts.
Using the wrong octet for the magic number — apply it to the interesting octet (where the mask is neither 0 nor 255).
Subnetting smallest-first in VLSM — wastes address space and breaks the larger segments; always largest first.
lessons.try_it: Subnet 10.20.0.0/22 on paper right now: list all subnets, then the usable range of the second one. Time yourself.

lessons.title: VLSM in Practice: Right-Sizing Every Segment
concepts: VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking) lets each segment use exactly the mask it needs — no more wasting a /24 on a point-to-point link that needs 2 addresses.
The ordering rule is absolute: sort requirements largest to smallest, allocate sequentially. A single out-of-order allocation fragments the space.
Point-to-point links get /30 (2 usable) or /31 (2 usable, no broadcast) per RFC 3021. Never assign a /24 to a WAN link — that is 252 wasted addresses.
Always leave growth room: size for current hosts + 20–50% unless the question says otherwise. Real networks grow; exam topologies usually state exact counts.
Document as you allocate: network, mask, usable range per segment in a table. The table IS the deliverable — in the exam and in production.

example.code:
Requirements: LAN-A 60 hosts, LAN-B 28 hosts, WAN link 2 hosts. Base: 192.168.1.0/24
  LAN-A (60) → /26: 192.168.1.0/26 (usable .1–.62)
  LAN-B (28) → /27: 192.168.1.64/27 (usable .65–.94)
  WAN (2) → /30: 192.168.1.96/30 (usable .97–.98)
  Remaining: 192.168.1.100–.255 free for growth
example.walkthrough: VLSM is bin-packing with IP addresses. The discipline — largest first, document everything — is what separates engineers from memorizers.

pitfalls: Allocating in the given order instead of sorted order — the #1 VLSM exam trap.
Forgetting /31 exists for point-to-point — know it, though /30 is the safe exam answer.
Overlapping allocations — the allocation table prevents this; no table, no confidence.
lessons.try_it: Do the worked example above on paper without looking, then compare. Repeat with different host counts until it is boring.

lessons.title: RF Fundamentals: What the Air Is Doing
concepts: Wi-Fi is radio: 2.4 GHz travels farther and penetrates better but has only 3 non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11) and more interference. 5 GHz has more channels and speed but shorter range.
Channel overlap is the silent killer: two APs on overlapping 2.4 GHz channels (e.g., 1 and 3) interfere worse than two sharing one channel, because they cannot coordinate airtime.
Signal math that matters: -30 dBm is excellent, -67 dBm is the voice/video floor, -80 dBm is nearly unusable. Every 3 dB is a doubling/halving of power.
AP placement follows the -67 dBm rule for the primary coverage area, with 15–20% cell overlap for roaming. More APs at lower power beats fewer APs at max power.
2.4 GHz is for IoT and legacy; steer clients to 5 GHz (band steering) for performance. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) adds clean spectrum where supported.

example.code:
Site survey reading: AP-3 shows -72 dBm in the conference room, channel 6.
  Diagnosis: weak signal (-72 < -67 floor) + possible co-channel contention.
  Fix: add AP or move AP-3 closer; verify no neighbor on channel 6 at high power.
example.walkthrough: Wireless troubleshooting starts with physics, not configuration. Check signal, channel, and interference before touching a single setting.

pitfalls: Cranking AP power to maximum — creates sticky clients that will not roam and interferes with neighbors.
Deploying on auto-channel without a survey — APs pick overlapping channels; plan channels deliberately.
Ignoring 2.4 GHz congestion — microwaves, Bluetooth, and baby monitors live there; it is a junk band for performance.
lessons.try_it: Sketch your home/office: mark AP locations, note which band each client uses, and identify one channel conflict to fix.

lessons.title: Enterprise WLAN Architecture
concepts: Enterprise WLAN = APs + wireless controller (physical, virtual, or cloud) + RADIUS for 802.1X. The controller centralizes config, roaming, and RF management.
802.1X with EAP-TLS (certificates) is the enterprise standard: per-user, per-device authentication with dynamic VLAN assignment. PSK is for guest and IoT, never for corporate.
Roaming works because the controller (or 802.11r/k/v) pre-shares key material: 802.11r fast transition for speed, 802.11k neighbor reports, 802.11v BSS transition management.
VLANs segment wireless traffic: corporate (802.1X, internal VLAN), guest (captive portal, isolated VLAN, rate-limited), IoT (PSK, restricted VLAN, ACL'd).
Monitoring is continuous: rogue AP detection, channel utilization, client health. A WLAN without monitoring is a WLAN you will troubleshoot blind.

example.code:
New hire onboarding flow:
  Device → SSID CORP → 802.1X EAP-TLS → RADIUS validates cert
  → dynamic VLAN 20 assigned → policies pushed → connected
  Guest: SSID GUEST → captive portal → VLAN 99 (internet-only, 5 Mbps cap)
example.walkthrough: Enterprise wireless is identity-driven networking. The SSID is just the door — 802.1X, RADIUS, and VLANs decide who walks through it and where they may go.

pitfalls: Using one PSK for all corporate users — one leak compromises everyone; 802.1X gives per-user credentials.
Flat wireless network (no VLANs) — guests and IoT on the corporate LAN is a breach waiting for a date.
No rogue AP detection — evil twins are trivial to deploy; detection is the only defense.
lessons.try_it: Diagram the three-SSID architecture (corporate/guest/IoT) with auth method and VLAN for each. Label the RADIUS role.

lessons.title: MPLS vs SD-WAN: The WAN Decision
concepts: MPLS gives private, SLA-backed, QoS-capable connectivity between sites — at high cost and low agility. The provider's core is a private club; you pay for membership.
SD-WAN builds an encrypted overlay across any transport (broadband, LTE, MPLS) with centralized policy: pick per-application paths by real-time quality, fail over in sub-seconds.

The real decision is control vs convenience: MPLS outsources the WAN brain to the carrier; SD-WAN keeps the brain in-house with software. Most enterprises now run hybrid: SD-WAN over broadband + MPLS for the sites that truly need SLAs.
QoS survives the transition but moves: MPLS honors provider QoS markings end-to-end; SD-WAN does per-tunnel QoS and application-aware routing at the edge.
Security changes shape: MPLS was 'private therefore trusted' (wrong, but common); SD-WAN is zero-trust by default — every tunnel encrypted, every site authenticated.

example.code:
3-site retail chain:
  MPLS-only: $4,500/mo, 45-day changes, carrier ticket for every policy tweak
  SD-WAN over broadband: $900/mo, zero-touch provisioning, app-aware failover
  Hybrid: SD-WAN everywhere + keep MPLS at HQ for the SLA-backed voice trunk
example.walkthrough: Never answer 'which WAN technology' with a product — answer with the trade-off: cost, agility, SLA need, and security model. That framing works for every exam and every architecture review.

pitfalls: Calling MPLS 'secure' because it is private — private is not encrypted; misconfigurations and provider access are real threats.
SD-WAN as 'just VPN' — the overlay, centralized policy, and app-aware routing are the point, not the encryption.
Ignoring underlay quality — SD-WAN cannot fix 300ms of bufferbloat; measure the transport first.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-row trade-off table (cost/agility/SLA/security) for MPLS vs SD-WAN vs hybrid. Use it to justify a choice for a 10-site company.

lessons.title: VPN Overlays and Tunneling Reality
concepts: Site-to-site VPN: IKE Phase 1 (peer authentication + secure channel) then Phase 2 (IPsec SAs for traffic). Miss either and the tunnel is down — troubleshoot in phase order.
GRE adds no encryption — it is encapsulation for routing protocols over IP. GRE over IPsec is the classic combo: GRE carries the routing, IPsec provides the armor.
DMVPN simplifies hub-and-spoke: spokes build dynamic tunnels to each other via NHRP, so spoke-to-spoke traffic skips the hub. One config pattern, many tunnels.
MTU is the silent VPN killer: encapsulation overhead (IPsec ~50-70 bytes) plus a 1500-byte underlay MTU = fragmentation. Set TCP MSS clamping (typically 1350-1380) on the tunnel.
Verify with the phase discipline: `show crypto isakmp sa` (Phase 1 up?) → `show crypto ipsec sa` (Phase 2 up, encaps/decaps incrementing?) — counters that do not move name the broken phase.

example.code:
Tunnel up but no traffic:
  Phase 1: up (peers authenticated)
  Phase 2: up, encaps incrementing, decaps stuck at 0
  Diagnosis: far end not returning traffic — check far-end ACLs/NAT, then MTU/MSS.
  The counter asymmetry IS the clue.
example.walkthrough: VPN troubleshooting is counter-reading, not guessing. The encaps/decaps counters tell you which direction broke — let them speak before you change anything.

pitfalls: Rebuilding the tunnel for a traffic problem — if Phase 1/2 are up, the tunnel is fine; the problem is policy or MTU.
Forgetting MSS clamping — the classic 'some sites load, large transfers hang' symptom.
GRE without IPsec for sensitive traffic — encapsulation is not encryption; label it correctly.
lessons.try_it: Write the 5-command VPN verification sequence for your platform (Cisco/Fortinet/Palo Alto) in phase order. Memorize the order.

lessons.title: Test-Day Protocol: The Final 24 Hours
concepts: No new material in the final 24 hours: review subnetting speed, the OSI cheat sheet, and exam strategy only.
Logistics: ID, confirmation, route, parking. Arrive 30 minutes early; breathe, don't cram.
Sleep 8 hours the last 2-3 nights. Subnetting speed comes from a rested brain.
During: budget time per question, flag-and-move on stuck PBQs, no blanks.

example.code: T-24h: [ ] subnetting drills (10, timed) [ ] ID + route [ ] 8h sleep [ ] strategy card
example.walkthrough: Trust the preparation. The final day is logistics and rest.

pitfalls: Cramming new topics.
All-nighter.
Skipping logistics.
lessons.try_it: Time 10 subnetting problems now. Record your average — that is your exam pace.

lessons.title: Supernetting and Route Summarization
concepts: Supernetting (route summarization) is subnetting in reverse: combine contiguous subnets into one larger advertisement. 192.168.0.0/24 + 192.168.1.0/24 = 192.168.0.0/23.
Why summarize: smaller routing tables, less update traffic, faster convergence. The internet runs on summarization — BGP would collapse without it.
The rule: summarize where the address plan allows — contiguous blocks with aligned boundaries. Good addressing plans summarize cleanly; bad ones don't.
Watch for discontiguous subnets: summarizing across a gap creates black holes (traffic for the gap goes nowhere). Summarize only what you actually own contiguously.
Exam pattern: 'which summary route covers these networks?' — find the common bits, count them, that is the prefix length. Binary is the honest method.

example.walkthrough: Summarization rewards good addressing plans and punishes bad ones. Design address space to summarize — future-you (and BGP) will thank you.

pitfalls: Summarizing discontiguous space — black holes for the gaps.
Over-summarization — advertising space you don't own attracts others' traffic.
Binary-free guessing — write the bits; the answer is in them.
lessons.try_it: Summarize 172.16.8.0/24 through 172.16.11.0/24. Show the binary work.

lessons.title: Wireless Troubleshooting Toolkit
concepts: The toolkit: spectrum analyzer (interference), survey mode (signal/heatmaps), client debugs (why did IT disconnect?), and packet capture (802.11 frames tell the truth).
Client-side first: does the CLIENT see the SSID? At what signal? Client drivers lie less than infrastructure dashboards — start where the pain is.
Common signatures: slow everywhere = interference or capacity; one area = coverage; one client = driver/config; intermittent = roaming or DFS events.
DFS channels (52-144): radar detection forces channel changes. If clients drop periodically on DFS channels, move to non-DFS or accept the radar dance.
Document the baseline: signal, SNR, channel utilization, client count per AP — when normal. Troubleshooting compares against baseline, not against hope.

example.code:
Ticket: 'WiFi slow in Building B, started Tuesday.'
  Check: channel utilization 85% (was 40%) — what changed Tuesday?
  Found: new AP on overlapping channel from the tenant next door.
  Fix: coordinate or move channels; document the baseline for next time.
example.walkthrough: 'What changed?' is the most powerful troubleshooting question. Baselines make it answerable.

pitfalls: Blaming the controller for a client driver bug — check the client side first.
Ignoring DFS behavior — periodic drops on DFS channels are radar, not ghosts.
No baseline — without normal, every number is just a number.
lessons.try_it: Write the 5-item wireless baseline for your environment. What is missing today?

lessons.title: SD-WAN Policy Design
concepts: Policy = business intent in rules: 'voice gets the best path, always; bulk backup uses whatever is cheapest; guest internet breaks out locally.' Write the intent before the config.
Path selection inputs: loss, latency, jitter per tunnel (measured continuously). Policy maps application SLAs to path quality — voice needs low jitter; backup needs bandwidth.
Failover design: sub-second for critical apps (pre-built standby tunnels), seconds for the rest. Test failover quarterly — untested failover is hope.
Security policy rides along: which traffic gets inspected where, encryption standards per tunnel, and the zero-trust posture (every site authenticated, every tunnel encrypted).
Start with 3 policies: critical (best path + fast failover), default (balanced), bulk (cheapest path). Complexity grows from there — earn it.

example.code:
Policy sketch:
  VOICE: prefer MPLS; failover to broadband if loss >1%; alert on failover.
  BUSINESS-APPS: best-quality tunnel; balance across both.
  BACKUP: cheapest path; deprioritize during business hours.
  GUEST: local internet breakout; never traverse WAN.
  Four lines that run the WAN.
example.walkthrough: Policy design is business translation: SLAs become path rules. Write the intent in English first; the config is just transcription.

pitfalls: Config before intent — clicking without the policy written down produces chaos.
No failover testing — the first real failover should not be during an outage.
One policy for everything — voice and backups have opposite needs; differentiate.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-line policy for a hypothetical 5-site company. What would you measure to validate it?

lessons.title: VLANs in Practice: Beyond the Basics
concepts: Access ports carry one VLAN (untagged); trunk ports carry many (tagged 802.1Q). The native VLAN on a trunk is untagged — change it from 1 and never use it for data.
Voice VLANs separate IP phones via CDP/LLDP-MED auto-assignment: one port, two VLANs (data + voice), QoS trust on the phone. The standard enterprise desk pattern.
VLAN pruning limits trunk traffic to needed VLANs: `switchport trunk allowed vlan` explicitly. Pruning reduces broadcast domains and is a security control, not just optimization.
Troubleshoot VLANs in order: correct VLAN on port? Trunk allowing it? Same subnet/gateway? SVI up? 90% of 'VLAN not working' is a port in the wrong VLAN.

example.code:
Phone + PC, one port:
  switchport mode access
  switchport access vlan 10        (data)
  switchport voice vlan 20         (voice, tagged via CDP)
  PC untagged on 10; phone tags 20. One cable, two networks.
example.walkthrough: VLANs are policy expressed in switching: who can talk to whom at L2. Design the policy first (the matrix), then configure.

pitfalls: Native VLAN 1 carrying data — the default every attacker knows; change and unused it.
Trunking to end devices — access ports for hosts, trunks for switches/APs only.
Forgetting the SVI/gateway — inter-VLAN routing needs a gateway per VLAN; L2 alone does not route.
lessons.try_it: Write the 4-command VLAN config for a new user port (data VLAN 30) from memory. Then the trunk config.

lessons.title: STP: Keeping Loops from Killing the LAN
concepts: STP exists because redundant links create loops, and loops create broadcast storms. One logical path active; the rest block — redundancy without meltdown.
Election: lowest bridge ID becomes root; every non-root picks the lowest-cost path to root (root port); per segment, one designated port forwards, rest block. The math is deterministic.
Port states: blocking → listening → learning → forwarding (30-50s classic STP). RSTP converges in seconds; MSTP maps VLANs to instances. Know which your exam expects.
PortFast for access ports (skip listening/learning — endpoints, not switches), BPDU Guard to kill PortFast ports receiving BPDUs (rogue switch defense). This pair is the exam favorite.
Root Guard protects the root placement: superior BPDUs on guarded ports put them in root-inconsistent state. Design the root deliberately (core/distribution), then guard it.

example.code:
New switch plugged into a wall jack:
  Without BPDU Guard: it participates in STP — could become root, chaos.
  With BPDU Guard on access ports: port goes err-disabled on first BPDU.
  Attack or accident, the LAN survives. Two commands, enormous protection.
example.walkthrough: STP is the LAN's immune system against loops: mostly invisible, absolutely critical. Configure the guards before you need them.

pitfalls: PortFast on trunk/uplink ports — creates temporary loops; PortFast is access-ports-only.
No BPDU Guard — one rogue switch can hijack the spanning tree.
Ignoring root placement — the oldest switch becomes root by default; design it instead.
lessons.try_it: List the STP port states in order with timers. Then write the PortFast + BPDU Guard config.

lessons.title: Routing Protocols: When to Use Which
concepts: Static routes: simple, predictable, zero overhead — for stub networks and defaults. Every static route is a promise you must keep manually.
OSPF (link-state): fast convergence, hierarchical areas, the enterprise standard. Routers share link states; each computes the shortest path (Dijkstra). Area 0 is the backbone — all areas touch it.
EIGRP (Cisco): hybrid, fast, simple — feasible successors give instant backup paths. Great in Cisco shops; irrelevant elsewhere.
BGP (path-vector): the internet's routing protocol. Policy-driven (not just shortest path), slow converging, infinitely scalable. eBGP between ASes, iBGP within.
Redistribution is where networks break: route feedback loops, metric mismatches. Redistribute with route-maps and tags, and only at designed boundaries.

example.code:
Branch design:
  Inside: OSPF single area (simple, converges fast)
  To HQ: eBGP (policy control, clean boundary)
  Default: static toward ISP with tracking
  Each protocol where it fits; redistribution only at the branch edge with tags.
example.walkthrough: Match the protocol to the problem: OSPF for enterprise interior, BGP for internet/policy boundaries, static for stubs. The exam tests the 'why', not just the 'what'.

pitfalls: OSPF across the internet — link-state does not scale to internet size; BGP does.
Redistribution without filters — feedback loops that melt networks; always tag and filter.
Single area OSPF for 500 routers — areas exist for scale; design them.
lessons.try_it: For a 3-site company, choose the routing design and justify each protocol choice in one sentence each.

lessons.title: SNMP and Network Monitoring
concepts: SNMP versions: v1/v2c use community strings (cleartext — sniffable); v3 adds auth + privacy (authPriv). In production, v3 or nothing — the exam agrees.
MIBs/OIDs are the vocabulary: 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 is sysUpTime. You do not memorize OIDs — you know that snmpwalk discovers them and templates map them.
Traps (device-initiated alerts) vs polling (manager-initiated queries): traps for events, polling for trends. Both — traps alone miss silent failures.
Baselines make monitoring meaningful: interface utilization, error counters, CPU/memory. Alert on deviation from baseline, not on absolute thresholds alone.
NetFlow/sFlow/IPFIX show WHO is talking: top talkers, protocols, conversations. When 'the network is slow', flows name the hog in seconds.

example.code:
Interface flapping diagnosis:
  SNMP poll: ifInErrors climbing on Gi0/1
  + syslog: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN every 2 min
  + NetFlow: traffic normal (not a load issue)
  Verdict: physical layer (cable/SFP), not congestion.
  Three sources, one conclusion — that is monitoring done right.
example.walkthrough: Monitor in layers: SNMP for health, syslog for events, flows for traffic. One source is a hint; three are a diagnosis.

pitfalls: SNMP v2c on the internet — community strings in cleartext; v3 with authPriv minimum.
No baselines — 'CPU at 60%' means nothing without knowing normal is 20%.
Alerting on everything — alert fatigue kills monitoring; alert on actionable, dashboard the rest.
lessons.try_it: List the 5 SNMP OIDs you would poll for a core switch and what each tells you.

lessons.title: Change Management for Networks
concepts: Every production change follows: request → risk assessment → approval → maintenance window → implement → verify → document. Skipping steps is how outages are manufactured.
Risk assessment asks: blast radius? rollback plan? tested where? A change without a tested rollback is a gamble, not a plan.
Maintenance windows exist for a reason: even 'harmless' changes get the window. The 2-minute firewall tweak at noon is the outage story everyone has.
Verify after EVERY change: the specific thing changed + neighbors (did we break anything adjacent?). Then document: what, when, by whom, why.
Emergency changes still get a paper trail: implement, then document within 24h with retroactive approval. 'Emergency' explains timing, not absence of process.

example.code:
Friday 5pm 'quick' VLAN change:
  Without process: typo in allowed-VLAN list → trunk drops 3 VLANs → Monday outage.
  With process: window scheduled, config diffed, rollback (previous config saved),
    verified per-VLAN after, documented.
  The process costs 20 minutes. The outage costs a weekend.
example.walkthrough: Change management is not bureaucracy — it is the checklist that prevents the 2 AM call. Professionals follow it especially when it feels unnecessary.

pitfalls: 'Too small to need a window' — the smallest changes cause the biggest outages (overconfidence).
No rollback plan — 'we'll figure it out' is not a plan; save the previous config first.
Undocumented emergency changes — the next engineer inherits a mystery; document within 24h.
lessons.try_it: Write a change request for a firewall rule addition: risk, blast radius, rollback, verification steps.

lessons.title: Firewall Rule Design
concepts: Rule order is everything: first match wins (most platforms). Place specific allows first, general denies after, explicit deny-all + log at the end. Order IS the policy.
Default deny, log all: the last rule denies everything and logs it. Those logs are your threat intel — denied traffic patterns reveal scans and misconfigurations.
Stateful inspection tracks connections: allow the outbound SYN, and the return traffic is automatically permitted. Stateless ACLs need explicit return rules — know which you are writing.
Object-based rules (address groups, service groups) beat raw IPs: 'WEB-SERVERS → APP-SERVERS : HTTPS' reads as policy; 10.1.2.0/24 → 10.1.3.0/24 : 443 reads as trivia.
Review cadence: quarterly rule audits, remove unused rules, verify business justification per rule. Rule bloat is a security debt that compounds.

example.code:
DMZ web server rules:
  1. ALLOW internet → web-vip : 80,443 (public service)
  2. ALLOW web-servers → db-vip : 5432 (app tier only)
  3. ALLOW mgmt-net → web-servers : 22 (jump host only)
  4. DENY all → log (the audit trail)
  Read top-to-bottom: each packet meets its fate at the first match.
example.walkthrough: Write rules as policy sentences first, then translate to syntax. If you cannot state the policy in words, the rule is wrong.

pitfalls: Any-any allow 'temporarily' — the most breached rule in history; time-box or refuse.
Wrong order (deny before allow) — first-match-wins makes order the entire game.
No logging on denies — blind to scans; the deny log is free threat intel.
lessons.try_it: Write 5 rules for a new internal app server (needs: user HTTPS, admin SSH from jump host, DB access). Order them correctly.

lessons.title: IDS/IPS Placement and Tuning
concepts: IDS detects (alerts); IPS prevents (blocks inline). Same engine, different placement: IDS on a SPAN port (sees copies), IPS inline (sees everything, can drop).
Placement: behind the firewall (sees what got through), before critical servers (last look), and at key segments. An IDS outside the firewall drowns in internet noise.
Tuning is the job: default rulesets false-positive constantly. Baseline for 2 weeks in IDS mode, tune out the noise, THEN consider IPS blocking. Block-on-day-one breaks business.
Signature (known bad) vs anomaly (deviation from baseline) vs heuristic: layer them. Signatures catch knowns; anomaly catches the novel — with more false positives.
Encrypted traffic blinds IDS/IPS: TLS inspection (with proper CA deployment and privacy controls) or endpoint-based detection fills the gap. Know what your sensor CANNOT see.

example.code:
Tuning workflow:
  Week 1-2: IDS mode, collect alerts
  Triage: true positive / benign / false positive
  Tune: suppress benign (documented), escalate true
  Week 3: enable blocking ONLY on high-confidence signatures
  Repeat monthly. Tuning is continuous, not a project.
example.walkthrough: An untuned IPS is a denial-of-service machine you installed yourself. Tune in detect-mode first; block only what you understand.

pitfalls: IPS blocking on day one — false positives become self-inflicted outages.
IDS outside the firewall — alert fatigue from internet background radiation.
Ignoring encrypted traffic blindness — 90%+ of traffic is TLS; plan for it.
lessons.try_it: Sketch IDS/IPS placement for a 3-zone network. Mark SPAN vs inline and justify each.

lessons.title: Network Access Control (NAC)
concepts: NAC enforces policy at connection time: authenticate the user/device, check compliance (patches, AV, encryption), then assign access (VLAN, ACL). No compliance, no (full) network.
802.1X is the gold standard: EAP-TLS (certificates) for corporate, with RADIUS making the decision and the switch/AP enforcing it. Credentials per device, not per network.
Profiling handles the headless: printers, cameras, IoT get identified by behavior/fingerprint and placed in restricted VLANs. Unknown devices default to quarantine, not trust.
Guest flows: captive portal, sponsored access, time-limited credentials — on an isolated VLAN with internet-only. Guest traffic never touches corporate segments.
Monitor mode first: deploy NAC in observe-only, learn what is really on the network (you will be surprised), then enforce. Day-one enforcement breaks the business.

example.code:
New laptop connects:
  1. 802.1X EAP-TLS → RADIUS validates cert
  2. Compliance check: patches current? disk encrypted? AV running?
  3. Compliant → VLAN 10 (corporate). Non-compliant → VLAN 99 (remediation).
  4. Printer connects: profiled as printer → VLAN 40 (IoT, restricted).
  Identity + health decide access — automatically.
example.walkthrough: NAC turns the network from a hallway into a bouncer: every device shows ID and health at the door. Deploy in monitor mode; the surprises teach you the real network.

pitfalls: Enforcement on day one — the unknown devices will break; monitor first, enforce after.
PSK for corporate users — one shared password is one leak from total compromise; 802.1X instead.
No profiling for IoT — headless devices need a policy too; quarantine-by-default.
lessons.try_it: Design the NAC policy matrix: device types × compliance states → VLAN/ACL. Cover 4 device types.

lessons.title: The OSI Troubleshooting Method
concepts: Troubleshoot by layer, in order: Physical (cables, link lights) → Data Link (MAC, VLAN, duplex) → Network (IP, gateway, routing) → Transport (ports, firewall) → Application (service, DNS, certs).
Bottom-up vs top-down: bottom-up (start at L1) when 'nothing works'; top-down (start at the app) when 'one thing fails'. Divide and conquer: ping the gateway to split L1-L3 from L4+.

The single most powerful command sequence: ipconfig/ifconfig (am I addressed?) → ping gateway (L2/L3 local OK?) → ping 8.8.8.8 (routing OK?) → nslookup (DNS OK?) → test the app. Each step isolates a layer.
Document as you go: what you tested, the result, what it ruled out. Troubleshooting without notes repeats tests and misses patterns.
Escalate with evidence: 'L1-L3 verified (ping gateway OK, no errors), DNS resolves, TCP 443 SYN gets no ACK — likely firewall' beats 'network is down'.

example.code:
'Can't reach the intranet':
  ipconfig → 169.254.x.x (APIPA!) — DHCP failed. Stop: L3.
  vs. ipconfig → 10.1.5.20 OK → ping gateway OK → nslookup fails.
  Different failure points, different fixes. The layer method finds it in 60 seconds.
example.walkthrough: Layer-by-layer is not slow — it is the fastest path because it eliminates whole categories per test. Random testing is what wastes hours.

pitfalls: Rebooting before diagnosing — destroys evidence and often 'fixes' nothing durably.
Skipping layers ('must be DNS' without checking IP first) — assumptions skip the actual broken layer.
No documentation — the next identical ticket starts from zero again.
lessons.try_it: Run the 5-command sequence on your machine now. Record each result and what layer it verified.

lessons.title: Wireshark: Reading the Wire
concepts: Capture filters (capture only what you need: `host 10.1.2.3 and port 443`) vs display filters (`tcp.flags.syn==1`). Capture narrow, display flexibly — disk fills fast on busy links.
The 3-way handshake in packets: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK. No SYN/ACK back = firewall or service down. RST instead of SYN/ACK = port closed. The handshake IS the connectivity test.
Follow TCP streams: right-click → Follow → TCP Stream reassembles the conversation. Reading the stream beats reading packets for application issues.
Expert info flags retransmissions, zero windows, resets: black/red entries are not decoration — each names a symptom (congestion, dead peer, refused connection).
Capture at both ends when possible: packets seen leaving A but not arriving at B = the path ate them (firewall, ACL, routing). One-sided captures guess; two-sided captures prove.

example.code:
App timeout diagnosis:
  Client sends SYN → no reply (3 SYNs, then give up).
  Not RST (would mean port closed) — silence means filtered.
  Verdict: firewall dropping, not service down.
  Three packets told the whole story.
example.walkthrough: Learn to read handshakes before anything else: SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK/RST patterns diagnose 80% of connectivity issues in seconds.

pitfalls: Capturing everything on a busy link — gigabytes of noise; filter at capture.
Ignoring expert info colors — the tool already flagged the anomalies; look at them.
One-sided capture conclusions — 'server never replied' needs the server-side capture to confirm.
lessons.try_it: Capture a page load (filter: tcp port 443). Find one complete handshake and one TLS ClientHello. Screenshot both.

lessons.title: Common Network Issues Cheat Sheet
concepts: APIPA (169.254.x.x) = DHCP failed: check DHCP server, scope exhaustion, VLAN, helper addresses. The address IS the diagnosis.
Duplex mismatch = slow + errors: auto/auto usually works; hard-code both sides identically if manual. Mismatches show as FCS errors and late collisions.
DNS fails but IP works = name resolution issue: check resolver config, test with nslookup/dig, verify the DNS server itself is reachable.
Intermittent = physical or STP: flapping links, duplex, spanning-tree reconvergence. Check interface error counters and logs for patterns.
Slow = congestion, duplex, or MTU: check utilization, errors, and path MTU. 'Slow' is a symptom — the counters name the disease.

example.code:
Symptom → first check:
  No IP (169.254) → DHCP scope/server/VLAN
  Slow + errors → duplex/speed mismatch
  Some sites fail → DNS or MTU
  Everything flaps → STP/physical
  One app fails → firewall port / service status
  Pattern-match first, then verify with data.
example.walkthrough: Experienced troubleshooters pattern-match symptoms to causes in seconds — then verify. Build your pattern library deliberately; this cheat sheet is the start.

pitfalls: Treating symptoms as causes — 'slow network' is never the diagnosis; find the counter that proves it.
Changing multiple things at once — one change, one test; otherwise you never learn what fixed it.
Forgetting to check the obvious — link lights, cable seating, 'is it plugged in' still solve tickets.
lessons.try_it: From the cheat sheet, write the 5 symptom→check pairs on a card. Keep it at your desk for a week.

lessons.title: OSI Model and Encapsulation
concepts: The OSI model's seven layers (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) give every network problem an address — troubleshooting is the art of finding the right floor.
Encapsulation: each layer wraps the payload with its header (and sometimes trailer) — data → segment (TCP) → packet (IP) → frame (Ethernet) → bits. Decapsulation reverses it at the destination.
The PDU names are exam currency: L4 segment/datagram, L3 packet, L2 frame, L1 bits — questions use them precisely.
TCP (connection-oriented, reliable, sequenced) vs UDP (connectionless, fast, best-effort): the choice follows the application's tolerance for loss vs delay.
Troubleshoot top-down or bottom-up systematically: 'works by IP, fails by name' = upper layers; 'no link light' = Layer 1 — never skip layers randomly.

example.code:
Sending 'HELLO':
  L7: data = 'HELLO'
  L4: + TCP header (ports, seq#)      → segment
  L3: + IP header (src/dst IP)       → packet
  L2: + Ethernet header/trailer (MACs, FCS) → frame
  L1: → bits on the wire
Receiving reverses: NIC checks FCS → IP checks dst → TCP orders by seq# → app reads 'HELLO'
example.walkthrough: Each header answers a question for its layer: TCP's ports identify the application, IP's addresses route across networks, Ethernet's MACs deliver across one link, the FCS detects corruption. The layer that can't answer its question is where the fault lives.

pitfalls: Memorizing the layer names without the PDU names and device mappings (hub=L1, switch=L2, router=L3) — the exam tests all three together.
Confusing TCP and UDP use cases: DNS and VoIP/streaming favor UDP; file transfer and web favor TCP.
Troubleshooting by guessing instead of isolating — 'reboot everything' is never the methodology answer.
lessons.try_it: Take a ping that fails. List one check per OSI layer, bottom-up, that isolates the fault — then run them on a real connectivity problem.

lessons.title: Cabling, Media, and Connectors
concepts: Copper categories: Cat5e (1 Gbps/100m), Cat6 (10 Gbps/55m), Cat6A (10 Gbps/100m) — pick by speed, distance, and PoE heat; the 100-meter limit includes patch cords.
Fiber: multimode (short, LED/laser, cheaper optics) vs single-mode (long-haul, laser, costlier) — distance and budget decide; connectors: LC (small, common), SC, ST, MPO for high-density.
TIA/EIA 568A vs 568B wiring standards — use one consistently; crossover cables (now largely replaced by Auto-MDIX) swap transmit/receive pairs.
EMI rules: keep copper away from power lines and fluorescent ballasts, respect bend radius, never kink fiber; plenum-rated cable where air-handling spaces require it.
PoE standards (802.3af/at/bt) deliver power with data — verify the switch's PoE budget covers all powered devices before deployment.

example.code:
Run plan for a 90m camera drop:
  Distance: 90m < 100m ✓ copper OK
  PoE++ (cameras + heaters): Cat6A (heat dissipation in bundles)
  Path crosses electrical room: reroute or use shielded (F/UTP)
  Termination: 568B both ends (straight-through), test with certifier
  Budget: camera 25W × 8 = 200W < switch 370W PoE budget ✓
example.walkthrough: Every line is a constraint check: distance against the 100m rule, cable category against PoE heat, path against EMI, termination standard for consistency, and power budget against the switch's capacity. Media implementation is constraint satisfaction, not brand shopping.

pitfalls: Exceeding 100m on copper (including patch cords at both ends) and blaming the switch for the resulting flakiness.
Mixing 568A and 568B terminations on one run — creates a crossover where you didn't want one.
Deploying PoE devices without checking the switch's total power budget — the last camera never powers on.
lessons.try_it: Terminate a Cat6 keystone jack to 568B, test with a cable verifier, and measure the full channel length — confirm it's under 100m.

lessons.title: Hardening the Network
concepts: Switch hardening: disable unused ports, enable port security (MAC limiting/sticky), DHCP snooping with trusted uplinks, Dynamic ARP Inspection, and BPDU guard on access ports.
802.1X port-based authentication with RADIUS ensures only authenticated devices (and users) get network access — the answer to 'rogue device on the LAN' questions.
Wireless hardening: WPA3-SAE (or WPA2-Enterprise), disable WPS, change defaults, segment guest/IoT traffic, and manage APs from a controller with rogue-AP detection.
Router/firewall hardening: change default credentials, disable unused services, use ACLs with least privilege, keep firmware patched, and log to a central SIEM.
Physical security counts: lock closets, secure console ports, and control who can plug into wall jacks — the exam treats physical access as a security boundary.

example.code:
Access-port hardening template:
  switchport mode access
  switchport port-security maximum 2
  switchport port-security violation restrict
  ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
  spanning-tree bpduguard enable
  authentication port-control auto   (802.1X via RADIUS)
example.walkthrough: Each line closes a specific attack: port-security caps MACs (stops CAM flooding and casual rogue devices), DHCP snooping rate-limits plus trusted-port design kills rogue DHCP, BPDU guard stops STP manipulation from access ports, and 802.1X requires authentication before the port forwards anything. Hardening is layered, like everything in security.

pitfalls: Enabling 802.1X without a working RADIUS server or a plan for printers/IoT (MAB) — you lock out the business, not just attackers.
Port security with 'shutdown' violation mode on user ports — one new phone MAC and the port dies until someone re-enables it; 'restrict' is usually safer.
Hardening the network while leaving default credentials on the APs and switches themselves.
lessons.try_it: Audit one switch: list unused ports, check for default credentials, and verify DHCP snooping and port security status.

lessons.title: The Troubleshooting Methodology
concepts: The CompTIA sequence: Identify the problem → Establish a theory → Test the theory → Establish a plan of action → Implement (or escalate) → Verify full functionality → Document findings.
Identify means gather: question users, check logs, note recent changes, duplicate the symptom — most 'mysteries' die at this step when someone checks the obvious.
Theorize from evidence, then test cheaply: question the obvious before the exotic, and change one variable at a time so you know what fixed it.
Common utilities map to layers: ping/traceroute (L3 reachability/path), ipconfig/ifconfig (addressing), nslookup/dig (DNS), netstat/ss (ports/connections), cable tester/loopback (L1).
Document everything: symptoms, theories tested, the fix, and preventive measures — documentation is a scored methodology step, not optional paperwork.

example.code:
Symptom: one user can't reach the intranet.
  Identify: link light off; only this user; worked yesterday.
  Theory: Layer 1 fault on this drop (cable/NIC/port).
  Test: swap cable → link up. (One variable changed.)
  Plan/Implement: replace the damaged cable.
  Verify: user reaches intranet; check for collateral issues.
  Document: ticket notes + replace aging cable batch in that office.
example.walkthrough: The methodology prevented a wild goose chase: the link light (identify) pointed at Layer 1, the single-variable test proved the cable, and verification plus documentation closed the loop. Skipping to 'reinstall the OS' would have wasted an hour and taught nothing.

pitfalls: Changing multiple things at once — you 'fix' it but never learn what was broken, and the exam penalizes this.
Skipping verification: the symptom disappears but the root cause persists (e.g., rebooting instead of replacing the failing cable).
Forgetting documentation — on the exam, 'document findings' is explicitly the final step and appears in answer choices.
lessons.try_it: Break something in a lab (unplug a cable, set a wrong mask). Troubleshoot it strictly in methodology order, writing down each step.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Packet's Journey
concepts: Every packet journey has the same acts: host builds it (encapsulation) → switch forwards the frame by MAC → router routes the packet by IP, rewriting the frame → NAT/firewall translate as needed → destination decapsulates.
MAC addresses are hop-local (rewritten at every router); IP addresses are end-to-end (preserved across the journey) — this single distinction unlocks switching vs routing questions.
ARP is the bridge between worlds: 'who has this IP?' asked on the local link, answered with a MAC — routers ARP for next hops, hosts ARP for gateways.
Return traffic mirrors the journey: the server replies to the source IP through its own gateway, and stateful devices (NAT, firewalls) recognize the return flow.
Trace any failure by walking the journey: where does the packet stop? The last device that had it names the fault domain.

example.code:
PC (10.1.1.10) → web server (203.0.113.80):
  PC: dst IP not local → ARP for gateway 10.1.1.1 → frame to gateway MAC
  Switch: forwards frame by MAC table
  Router: strips frame, routes by dst IP, builds NEW frame to next hop
  Firewall: state table entry created, NAT src → public IP
  ISP routers: hop-by-hop MAC rewrite, IP preserved
  Server: decapsulates → app responds; return path mirrors back
example.walkthrough: Watch the two addressing schemes diverge: the frame's MACs change at every router (local delivery vehicles), while the packet's IPs stay constant (the end-to-end passport). NAT is the one place the source IP changes — a deliberate, stateful exception the firewall tracks so replies find their way home.

pitfalls: Thinking MAC addresses travel end-to-end — they don't; each router re-frames.
Forgetting ARP: 'host can't reach its gateway' is often just a failed or poisoned ARP, not a routing problem.
Ignoring the return path — asymmetric or blocked return traffic breaks connections that look fine outbound.
lessons.try_it: Run traceroute to a distant site. For each hop, state which header changed (MAC) and which didn't (IP) — narrate the journey out loud.

lessons.title: The 60-Second Subnetting Cheat Sheet
concepts: Memorize the CIDR block-size table for the interesting octet: /24=1, /25=128, /26=64, /27=32, /28=16, /29=8, /30=4 — block size = 256 − mask value.
Two formulas solve everything: subnets = 2^(borrowed bits), usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2. Borrowed = new mask − old mask.
For 'which subnet does this IP belong to': find the interesting octet, compute block size, count blocks from zero to bracket the address.
During the pre-exam tutorial (clock not running), dump the table and formulas onto the scratch sheet — then it's pure arithmetic under pressure.
Drill target: any standard subnetting question in under 30 seconds. Speed here buys minutes for PBQs.

example.code:
Q: Subnet, broadcast, and range for 172.16.88.99/20?
  Interesting octet: 3rd (mask 255.255.240.0). Block size = 256−240 = 16.
  Blocks: 0,16,32,48,64,80,96 → 88 falls in 80.
  Subnet: 172.16.80.0 | Broadcast: 172.16.95.255 (next block − 1)
  Usable: 172.16.80.1 − 172.16.95.254  (20 seconds)
example.walkthrough: No binary needed: block size gives the subnet boundaries, the next block minus one gives the broadcast, and .1/first to last-minus-one gives the usable range. The whole question reduces to counting by 16s.

pitfalls: Counting the network and broadcast as usable hosts — the −2 exists for exactly this trap.
Borrowing bits from /24 when the question gives a different starting mask (e.g., subnetting a /20).
Doing binary longhand on exam day — it's accurate but too slow; the block-size method is the exam technique.
lessons.try_it: Dump the /24–/30 block-size table from memory in under 60 seconds. Then solve 10 random subnetting questions against a 30-second timer.

lessons.title: PBQ Tactics: Wiring and Diagrams
concepts: Network+ PBQs cluster around: wiring diagrams (media by constraint), device placement (AP/switch/router in a topology), CLI troubleshooting (spot the misconfiguration), and port/protocol matching.
Wiring PBQ method: for each run, name the governing constraint — distance (>100m = fiber), EMI (fiber), PoE/heat (Cat6A), ISP handoff (fiber) — then place and re-verify.
CLI PBQ method: read the config line by line against the symptom; the fault is usually one wrong value (mask, gateway, VLAN, duplex) — diff the config against the requirement.
Partial credit is generous: place everything you can reason about, make your best guess on the rest — blanks score zero.
Do PBQs in the second pass: bank the quick multiple-choice points first, then spend your remaining time where partial credit rewards careful work.

example.code:
PBQ: place devices in a branch diagram.
  'Connects 3 VLANs, routes between them' → Layer 3 switch or router
  'Extends wireless to warehouse aisle' → AP with directional antenna
  'Connects branch to ISP' → edge router at the demarc
  Verify: does each device's capability match its job? (AP doesn't route VLANs.)
example.walkthrough: Each placement is a job description matched to a device's capabilities. The verification pass catches the classic trap — placing a Layer 2 switch where inter-VLAN routing is required. Reason from function, not from what 'looks right' in the diagram.

pitfalls: Placing devices by familiarity instead of by the stated requirement — re-read each label's job description.
Leaving PBQ slots empty out of perfectionism — partial credit rewards attempted reasoning.
Burning 15 minutes on one PBQ while 20 quick questions wait — time-box and return.
lessons.try_it: Draw a small office floor plan. Label 6 runs/devices with constraints, then have a study partner place media and devices — grade each other's reasoning.

lessons.title: Question Patterns and Distractor Traps
concepts: 'MOST likely' = weigh the evidence: the answer is the cause best supported by ALL the clues, not the scariest or most technical option.
'FIRST'/'NEXT' = methodology order: information-gathering beats action; identify before theory, theory before test, containment of evidence before fixes.
'BEST' = optimize for the stated goal: cheapest, fastest, most secure, least disruptive — the goal word in the question picks the winner among plausible options.
Distractor patterns: the exact-wrong-value (off-by-one mask), the right-concept-wrong-layer (VLAN for a Layer 1 symptom), and the overkill option (replace the router for a bad cable).
Absolute words ('always,' 'never') in answer choices are usually wrong — real networks are conditional, and the exam knows it.

example.code:
Q: 'Link light off, one user affected. MOST likely cause?'
  A) Faulty NIC/cable  B) VLAN misconfiguration  C) DNS failure  D) Duplex mismatch
  Evidence: link light OFF = Layer 1 verdict → B, C, D all need link UP.
  Answer: A — the evidence eliminates everything above Layer 1.
example.walkthrough: The pattern: each clue is a filter. 'Link light off' filters out every answer above Layer 1; 'one user' filters out switch-wide faults. What's left standing after the filters is the answer — you barely need to know what a duplex mismatch is.

pitfalls: Choosing the most technical-sounding answer when the evidence points at something simple — the exam rewards evidence, not sophistication.
Ignoring the goal word (BEST/cheapest vs BEST/most secure) — two options can both 'work' while only one fits the stated optimization.
Second-guessing filtered answers back in — if the evidence eliminated it, keep it eliminated.
lessons.try_it: Take 10 practice questions. Before answering, write the goal word and list which clues eliminate which options — answer from the eliminations.

lessons.title: VLSM Design From Scratch
concepts: VLSM lets each subnet use a different mask, sized to its host count — the alternative (one mask for all) wastes addresses on small subnets and starves large ones.
Design order is largest-first: sort requirements descending, allocate each from where the last ended — this prevents fragmentation that strands unusable gaps.
Size each block: hosts needed → next power of 2 ≥ hosts+2 (network+broadcast) → prefix length = 32 − exponent. 100 hosts → 128 → /25.
Track allocation on paper: network address, mask, usable range, broadcast — then the next block starts at the previous broadcast + 1.
Reserve growth and point-to-point links explicitly: WAN links get /30 (or /31); always leave an unallocated block for the requirement you forgot.

example.walkthrough: Largest-first keeps the blocks packed: each allocation starts exactly where the previous broadcast ended. The +2 in the sizing accounts for network and broadcast addresses — the classic off-by-one that undersizes LAN-A to a /27 (30 hosts) and breaks the design. Note the reserved tail: real designs leave room.

pitfalls: Forgetting the +2 (network and broadcast) when sizing — 60 hosts needs 62 addresses minimum, which is a /26, not a /27.
Allocating smallest-first, which fragments the space and strands gaps too small for the big LANs.
Overlapping blocks from arithmetic slips — always verify: next network = previous broadcast + 1.
lessons.try_it: Design VLSM for 10.5.0.0/22 with: 400 hosts, 180 hosts, 90 hosts, 40 hosts, and 4 WAN links. Verify no overlaps.

lessons.title: RF Essentials: Channels, Power, and Antennas
concepts: 2.4 GHz: only channels 1, 6, 11 are non-overlapping — everything else interferes with its neighbors; 5 GHz offers many non-overlapping 20/40/80 MHz channels (minus DFS radar channels near airports).
Channel width trades speed for airtime: wider channels (40/80/160 MHz) are faster but consume more spectrum and suffer more interference — 20 MHz is often right for dense 2.4 GHz.
Power tuning: match AP transmit power to client power so cells are symmetric; too much power creates sticky clients and co-channel interference, too little creates dead zones.
Antennas shape coverage: omnidirectional for open areas, directional (patch/yagi) for aisles and point-to-point bridges, MIMO/multiple streams for throughput.
The exam's RF math is light but real: know dBm direction (higher = stronger), the −67 dBm design target for voice/data, and that 3 dB ≈ double/halve power.

example.code:
Dense office, 12 APs:
  2.4 GHz radios: channels 1, 6, 11 reused in a honeycomb pattern, 20 MHz width, medium power
  5 GHz radios: non-DFS channels 36–48, 149–165, 40 MHz width
  Survey target: −67 dBm cell edge, 15–20% cell overlap for roaming
  Result: no co-channel neighbors within earshot, clean handoffs
example.walkthrough: The honeycomb reuses the only three non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels so adjacent APs never share one; 5 GHz gets the wide-open non-DFS channels; medium power keeps cells tight enough that clients roam instead of clinging. Every choice serves the −67 dBm edge target with overlap for handoffs.

pitfalls: Leaving all APs on auto-channel at full power — they cluster on channel 6 and shout over each other.
Using 40 MHz channels in 2.4 GHz in dense areas — you consume two of the three clean channels and interfere with everything.
Deploying high-gain omnis to 'fix' a dead zone — gain reshapes coverage; it doesn't fill holes behind obstructions.
lessons.try_it: With a Wi-Fi analyzer app, map your space: note channels in use, signal at the farthest seat, and whether 1/6/11 discipline is being followed.

lessons.title: SD-WAN and QoS at the Edge
concepts: SD-WAN replaces static WAN routing with centralized, application-aware policy: the controller steers traffic per-app across MPLS, broadband, and LTE based on real-time link measurements.
Path selection inputs: loss, latency, jitter measured continuously per tunnel — voice goes to the low-jitter path, bulk to the high-bandwidth path, automatically and per-packet if needed.
QoS chain: classify at the trusted edge → mark (DSCP EF for voice, AF for video/data classes) → queue (LLQ priority for voice, CBWFQ for classes) → police/shape to bounds.
Zero-touch provisioning lets branches deploy with an unboxed edge device that pulls config from the controller — the exam contrasts this with manual CLI staging.
Security rides along: SD-WAN builds encrypted overlays (IPsec) across untrusted broadband, so the 'cheap link' gets enterprise-grade confidentiality.

example.code:
Branch policy:
  voice (dscp ef): prefer MPLS; failover to broadband if loss <1% & jitter <30ms; LLQ priority 2 Mbps
  video (dscp af41): prefer broadband; MPLS backup
  bulk replication: broadband only, deprioritized, capped 50 Mbps
  guest wifi: broadband, rate-limited, direct internet breakout
example.walkthrough: Each application's sensitivity maps to a path and a queue: voice gets the stable path plus priority queuing because jitter kills calls; bulk gets the fat pipe but capped so it can't crowd out interactive traffic; guest traffic never touches the expensive MPLS. The controller enforces this continuously, not just at config time.

pitfalls: Marking traffic but never trusting/enforcing markings end-to-end — an EF mark the WAN ignores is decoration.
Giving voice priority without a policer — a voice flood (or misclassification) can starve all other traffic.
Treating SD-WAN as 'just VPN' — the differentiator is centralized policy plus dynamic, measured path selection.
lessons.try_it: Classify your home traffic into 4 classes (real-time, interactive, bulk, background). Write the marking and queuing policy you'd apply at your router.
