labs.title: Map the path — ping and traceroute
labs.objective: Verify reachability with ping, then use traceroute to list every hop and identify where a path breaks.
steps: This lab reworks the Network Troubleshooting scenarios 'Where do you ping first?' and 'Where do the packets die?' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ping -c 4 192.168.1.1 — four echo requests to the gateway; watch for Reply lines and 0% packet loss
Type exactly: traceroute 203.0.113.8 — each hop prints in order with round-trip times; asterisks mark hops that do not answer
Read the last responding hop before the timeouts — say in your own words which device or provider owns the fault.
Type exactly: ping -c 4 127.0.0.1 — the loopback baseline: if this ever fails, the fault is your own stack, not the network.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `ping -c 4 192.168.1.1`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "0% packet loss".
In the Terminal tab, run `traceroute 203.0.113.8`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "hop".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you test inside out and read the exact hop where paths die. Vague WAN tickets fear you now.

labs.title: Interrogate DNS — nslookup and dig
labs.objective: Query DNS directly with nslookup and dig, read which server answered, and distinguish record problems from server problems.
steps: This lab reworks the Network Troubleshooting scenario 'The name that will not resolve' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: nslookup intranet.lab.local — note the Server line (who answered) and the Address lines (what it returned)
Type exactly: dig intranet.lab.local — the ANSWER SECTION shows the record; the SERVER line shows who answered
Type exactly: dig intranet.lab.local MX — ask for mail exchanger records to see record-type selection in action
In your own words, say how you would tell 'the record is missing' apart from 'the client is asking the wrong server'.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `nslookup intranet.lab.local`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "Server".
In the Terminal tab, run `dig intranet.lab.local`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "ANSWER SECTION".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you question DNS directly instead of guessing. The phone book has no secrets from you.

labs.title: Read the host — ip addr and ss
labs.objective: Read interface addressing with ip addr and list listening sockets with ss, mapping ports to services.
steps: Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ip addr — find the inet line: it shows the IPv4 address with its prefix length (e.g., 192.168.1.44/24)
From that prefix length, say the subnet mask and network address in your own words
Type exactly: ss -tuln — listening TCP and UDP sockets, numeric — the modern replacement for netstat
Match each listening port to a service: 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS, 80/443 are web — say what an unexpected open port would prompt you to do.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `ip addr`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "inet ".
In the Terminal tab, run `ss -tuln`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "LISTEN".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — addressing and listening sockets read at a glance. You see the host the way the network sees it.

labs.title: Subnet on the wire — calculate and prove
labs.objective: Given a host address with a prefix length, compute the network address and broadcast address, then verify connectivity reasoning.
steps: This lab turns the Network Implementation subnetting scenarios into a drill you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ip addr — the lab host shows inet 192.168.10.77/27
On paper or in your head: /27 means a 32-address block; 77 falls in the 64-95 block, so the network address is 192.168.10.64 and broadcast is 192.168.10.95
Type exactly: echo 192.168.10.64 — submit the network address you computed
Type exactly: echo 192.168.10.95 — submit the broadcast address you computed
Type exactly: ping -c 2 192.168.10.94 — the last usable host in the subnet; a reply proves your range math describes a real, reachable subnet.

checks.hint: Compute the /27 network address for 192.168.10.77/27, then in the Terminal tab run `echo 192.168.10.64` with your answer. Block size 32; which block holds 77?
Compute the /27 broadcast address for 192.168.10.77/27, then in the Terminal tab run `echo 192.168.10.95` with your answer. It is the last address of the block.
In the Terminal tab, run `ping -c 2 192.168.10.94`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "0% packet loss".

labs.success_message: Lab complete — network, broadcast, and last usable host computed and proven. Subnetting is now a skill, not a formula.

labs.title: Trust but verify — the ARP table
labs.objective: Inspect the ARP table with ip neigh, recognize a healthy gateway mapping, and spot the fingerprint of ARP spoofing.
steps: This lab reworks the Network Security scenario 'The poisoned cache' into commands you run yourself.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.
Type exactly: ip neigh — the neighbor table: each IP maps to exactly one MAC in the REACHABLE state
Find the gateway entry (192.168.1.1) and note its single MAC address — that is the healthy baseline
Now imagine a second machine claiming the same gateway IP with a different MAC — say in your own words what attack that is and which switch feature stops it

simulations.title: The VLAN that leaked
simulations.brief: After a switch replacement, voice phones work but PCs on the data VLAN cannot reach the internet. The old switch did this fine. Work the evidence in order.

steps.symptom: Phones (VLAN 20) work. PCs (VLAN 10) get no DHCP and cannot reach the gateway.
evidence: ipconfig (PC)

IPv4: 169.254.44.10
Gateway: (none)
Switch port status

Gi0/1 (to router): access VLAN 1
Gi0/2-24: access VLAN 10
options: Replace the router — it must have failed during the swap
The uplink to the router is an access port instead of an 802.1Q trunk — reconfigure Gi0/1 as a trunk carrying VLANs 10 and 20
Assign static IPs to all PCs
Reboot the phones to free up DHCP leases
steps.explain: The PCs' APIPA addresses say DHCP never reached them, and the port evidence shows why: the router uplink is an access port in VLAN 1, so tagged VLAN 10/20 traffic has no path to the router. The fix is an 802.1Q trunk on the uplink carrying both VLANs — the phones worked only because voice traffic was already handled elsewhere.

steps.symptom: Uplink is now a trunk, but PCs still get no DHCP. The router's subinterfaces exist for both VLANs.
evidence: Trunk status
Gi0/1: trunk, allowed VLANs: 1
Router subinterfaces
options: The trunk is the problem — convert it back to access
Add VLANs 10 and 20 to the trunk's allowed list — pruning is dropping the tagged frames
Replace the DHCP server
Change the PCs to VLAN 1
steps.explain: The trunk exists but its allowed-VLAN list contains only VLAN 1 — classic over-pruning. Tagged frames for 10 and 20 are dropped at the trunk. Adding the VLANs to the allowed list completes the path: PC -> access port (VLAN 10) -> trunk -> router subinterface -> DHCP.

steps.symptom: PCs now receive 192.168.10.x addresses and reach the internet. Phones still work.
evidence: ipconfig (PC)
options: Close the ticket — connectivity is restored
Verify DHCP, routing, and voice quality on a sample of each VLAN, then document the trunk and allowed-VLAN configuration
Remove VLAN 20 since the phones worked without the trunk
Set all ports back to access VLAN 1 for simplicity
steps.explain: Verify both VLANs fully — addressing, gateway reachability, and voice quality — because the swap touched shared infrastructure. Then document the trunk config and allowed VLANs so the next replacement does not repeat the outage. Connectivity restored is not the same as verified and documented.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed a trunking failure in two layers: missing trunk, then pruned trunk. VLAN problems are almost always about what the trunk carries — check mode first, allowed list second.

simulations.title: Half the office is offline
simulations.brief: Monday 9 a.m.: half the office cannot get on the network. The other half is fine. The weekend brought twenty new hires with laptops.

steps.symptom: Affected machines show 169.254.x.x; unaffected machines hold 10.1.1.x leases.
evidence: DHCP scope
Timeline
20 new laptops joined Friday afternoon
options: The switch is failing — replace it
Scope exhaustion from the new hires — shorten lease time, reconcile stale leases, expand the scope
The ISP is down for half the office
Reinstall NIC drivers on all affected machines
steps.explain: Twenty new devices against one free lease is arithmetic, not mystery: the scope is exhausted. Old leases keep working while newcomers get APIPA — the exact fingerprint. Shorten leases so stale ones expire, reconcile the ghosts, and expand the scope for headroom.

steps.symptom: Scope expanded to a /23 and leases shortened, but three machines still show APIPA after renewing.
evidence: ipconfig (stubborn PC)
Switch port
Gi0/17: err-disabled
options: Expand the scope again — it must still be exhausted
The port is err-disabled (likely a port-security violation or loop) — investigate the port, clear the cause, re-enable it
Replace those three PCs
Disable DHCP and go static everywhere
steps.explain: Err-disabled is the switch protecting itself — typically a port-security violation, a loop, or excessive errors. The port is administratively down, so no DHCP conversation can happen on it. Find the cause (rogue switch? too many MACs?), clear it, and re-enable the port; the scope fix already solved everyone else.

steps.symptom: All machines now hold 10.1.x.x leases and reach the network. The err-disabled port was a new hire's travel switch creating a loop.
evidence: Scope
Port Gi0/17
up, single MAC, STP blocking the loop port
options: Close the ticket
Verify a sample of previously affected machines, enable STP loop protection where missing, and document the new scope and lease policy
Ban personal switches with no written policy
Extend leases back to 30 days
steps.explain: Two root causes, two preventions: scope sizing and lease policy for the exhaustion, STP loop guard for the travel switch. Verify the sample, harden the edge against loops, and document — otherwise the next hiring wave replays the morning.

simulations.debrief: You read APIPA's fingerprint twice — once for exhaustion, once for a dead port — and fixed causes, not symptoms. Scoping by 'who works and who does not' is the whole game.

simulations.title: The slow WAN
simulations.brief: The branch's WAN link tests at full speed at 6 a.m. but crawls every afternoon. The carrier insists their circuit is clean.

steps.symptom: 6 a.m.: 95 Mbps. 2 p.m.: 8 Mbps with high latency. No errors on the carrier handoff.
evidence: Utilization graph

06:00 12% util
14:00 98% util, latency 240ms
Top talkers 14:00
Backup server -> offsite: 78 Mbps
options: The carrier is lying — escalate aggressively
Afternoon backups saturate the link — the pattern is utilization, not a fault; reschedule or rate-limit backups and consider QoS
Replace the branch router
Upgrade the LAN switches
steps.explain: The utilization graph is the diagnosis: the link is fine at 6 a.m. and saturated at 2 p.m. by backups. A fault would not keep office hours. The fix is traffic management — move backups off-hours, rate-limit them, and protect interactive traffic with QoS — not new hardware.

steps.symptom: Backups rescheduled to midnight, but afternoons still show 60% utilization with bursty latency spikes.
evidence: Interface counters

FCS errors rising on the WAN port
Collisions: 0 (full duplex)
Speed/duplex
Router: auto | Provider CPE: 100/full forced
options: The backups are still running — reschedule again
Duplex mismatch between auto-negotiating router and forced-full provider CPE — match the settings (both auto or both forced)
The cable is too long
Buy a bigger WAN circuit
steps.explain: Rising FCS errors with zero collisions on a full-duplex link is the duplex-mismatch fingerprint: the auto side fell back to half-duplex while the forced side stays full, so one's transmissions look like errors to the other. Matching both sides to auto (or both forced identically) clears it — a configuration fix, not a capacity problem.

steps.symptom: Duplex matched, backups at midnight, afternoons now run at 35% utilization with 18ms latency. Users report the link feels new.
evidence: Utilization graph

14:00 35% util, latency 18ms
00:00 backup window: 88% util
options: Close the ticket — performance is restored
Verify with a week of monitoring against the new baseline, document the backup window and duplex standard, and set a utilization alert threshold
Keep tuning — 35% is still too high
Remove the QoS policy since the link is fast now
steps.explain: One good afternoon is not a baseline: monitor for a week to confirm the pattern holds, document the backup window and the duplex standard so the next device swap does not reintroduce the mismatch, and set an alert before utilization creeps back up. Prevention is the last methodology step for a reason.

simulations.debrief: You separated utilization from faults, read FCS errors as a duplex fingerprint, and closed with baselines and alerts. Performance troubleshooting is measurement plus pattern recognition.
